Title: A Generative AI-Based Didactic Tool for Inventory Learning in Accounting Education: Evidence from XP Contable
Source title: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
Affiliations: Institución Universitaria ITM, Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia
Authors with affiliations: Ospina D.P., Institución Universitaria ITM, Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia; Gaviria D.A.G., Institución Universitaria ITM, Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia; Luján S.A.S., Institución Universitaria ITM, Antioquia, Medellín, Colombia
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for accounting education, but empirical evidence on its use in structured, topic-specific interventions remains limited, particularly in inventory accounting. Accordingly, this study evaluated changes in inventory learning outcomes and student self-perceptions following the use of XP Contable—a GenAI-supported learning environment—among undergraduate students enrolled in the Financial Resources Accounting course. A pre-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design was used to obtain preliminary evidence of change in an intact classroom cohort. Twenty-one students constituted the final analytical sample. The structured classroom intervention comprised two two-hour sessions (four hours total), while platform access and practice extended over approximately three weeks. XP Contable integrated conceptual explanations, worked examples, AI-supported practice, assessment, immediate feedback, and repeated attempts. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, effect sizes, platform learning analytics, and descriptive thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Mean knowledge scores increased from 7.81 to 8.76 out of 11, t(20) = 2.42, p =.025, with a consistent Wilcoxon result (p =.026) and a moderate within-participant effect (Cohen’s dz =.53). Platform analytics recorded 466 assessment attempts, with mean performance increasing from 3.51 out of 5 on first attempts to 4.99 on best attempts (p <.001). The proportion of students reporting medium or high inventory knowledge increased from 38.1% to 81.0%. The largest increases in correct responses were observed for items addressing inventory valuation methods, periodic and perpetual inventory systems, and the cost-of-goods-sold formula. However, students continued to experience difficulty applying FIFO under rising prices and connecting ending inventory with financial statements. The findings provide preliminary evidence that a structured GenAI-supported learning environment can complement inventory instruction through repeated practice and feedback. However, the one-group design, small single-course sample, and absence of a control group limit causal inference and generalizability. © The Authors.

Title: An Explainable Human-Centered Federated Generative Intelligent Tutoring System for Sustainable Education
Source title: 7th International Conference on Inventive Research in Computing Applications, ICIRCA 2026 - Proceedings
Affiliations: Sri Venkateswara College of Engineering, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Karkambadi, Tirupati, India

Abstract: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) play a vital role in sustainable education by enabling adaptive and personalized learning. However, current ITS systems have limited explainability, low level of personalization, privacy issues and lack of real-time adaptation of the learner. The majority of existing systems are based on traditional machine learning models that are not able to adequately model complex behaviour and interactions of learners. This paper presents a Federated Learning (FL) based Human-Centered Federated Generative Intelligent Tutoring System (HFG-ITS), which combines Federated Learning (FL), Transformer based Generative AI (GPT), Reinforcement Learning (RL), Knowledge Graphs (KG), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to address these challenges. The proposed framework is based on the principles of decentralized training, generating dynamic personalized learning paths and adaptive interventions, while maintaining the privacy of the learner. Improved transparency and instructor trust is gained by incorporating SHAP-based explainability. Experimental testing on online educational datasets shows that the results are better with 98.74% accuracy, 98.21% F1-score and a 34.6% decrease in dropout prediction error compared to the existing ITS models. Moreover, the engagement of learners was enhanced by 29.4%, indicating the efficacy of the framework to create secure, explainable and scalable sustainable learning environments. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Reconceptualizing learning sciences in the era of artificial intelligence: Toward hybrid intelligence and adaptive learning systems
Source title: Acta Psychologica
Affiliations: University of Management and Technology (UMT), Lahore, Pakistan
Authors with affiliations: Malik A., University of Management and Technology (UMT), Lahore, Pakistan; Bashir I., University of Management and Technology (UMT), Lahore, Pakistan
Abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming education through intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, and large language models. However, research on Learning Sciences, AI in Education, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, and Hybrid Intelligence has largely progressed across partially separate research streams, resulting in fragmented theoretical perspectives and limited conceptual integration. This systematic review aims to synthesize the existing literature and develop an evidence-informed Hybrid Intelligence Framework that explains the relationships among Learning Sciences, AI technologies, learning analytics, and adaptive learning systems. Design/Methodology/Approach: A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature published between 2004 and March 2026 was retrieved through a focused, intersection-based search across seven databases: Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar. Following duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 32 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were synthesized using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis. Findings: Four interrelated themes emerged from the thematic synthesis: (1) epistemological fragmentation within Learning Sciences, (2) theory–technology contradictions between pedagogical theories and AI-supported educational systems, (3) the datafication of learning through learning analytics and adaptive technologies, and (4) Hybrid Intelligence as an emerging educational paradigm emphasizing collaboration among learners, educators, and intelligent systems. Building on these themes, the review proposes a Hybrid Intelligence Framework that integrates Learning Sciences, Artificial Intelligence, Learning Analytics, and adaptive learning systems into a coherent conceptual model for human-centred, ethical, explainable, and evidence-informed AI-supported education. Originality/Value: This review advances the literature by moving beyond isolated examinations of AI technologies or learning theories to provide an integrative conceptual synthesis of their interrelationships. The proposed Hybrid Intelligence Framework offers a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical research, instructional design, educational policy, and the development of adaptive learning environments that integrate human expertise with artificial intelligence while supporting learner agency and pedagogical integrity. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V. Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI)-based educational platforms are increasingly used in higher education to support academic organization and self-regulated learning. This study describes user experience, adoption barriers, and self-regulated learning indicators associated with implementing an AI tool that assists students with academic planning and the development of self-regulation skills. The tool combines generative models and learning analytics to deliver personalized recommendations, improve time management, and encourage effective study habits. Fifty students participated; 19 reported using the tool and 31 reported not using it. Among users, perceived usability and integration were high: 84.2% indicated that platform functions were well integrated and 79.0% reported that the tool was easy to use. Confidence and intention to continue were also favorable, with 89.5% reporting that they felt confident using the tool, were interested in frequent continued use, and believed that most people could learn it quickly. Regarding self-regulated learning, 84.2% reported being able to understand and learn both basic and difficult content, and 78.5% felt capable of achieving self-set goals. However, sustained planning behaviors were less consistent: 68.4% reported keeping up with studying through a structured schedule, whereas 26.3% reported studying only before exams. Procrastination-related execution difficulties were common (42.1% delaying non-preferred tasks; 36.8% struggling to start important tasks; 31.6% waiting until the last moment for deadlines). Study strategies suggested room for improvement (42.1% relying on repetition; 15.8% memorizing without understanding). Overall, the tool was positively appraised for usability and integration, while highlighting opportunities to strengthen sustained planning and deeper learning strategies in future deployments. © 2026 Latin American and Caribbean Consortium of Engineering Institutions. Title: A multilayered analysis of university students’ experiences with human and AI-based feedback: A comparative examination of BERTopic, LLM models, and mixture of agents approaches
Source title: Thinking Skills and Creativity
Affiliations: Prof. Necmettin Erbakan University, Eregli Faculty of Education, Department of Educational Science, Konya, Turkey; Prof. Izmir Institute of Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, İzmir, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Yildiz Durak H., Prof. Necmettin Erbakan University, Eregli Faculty of Education, Department of Educational Science, Konya, Turkey; Onan A., Prof. Izmir Institute of Technology, Department of Computer Engineering, İzmir, Turkey
Abstract: This study presents a multilayered text analysis framework for examining university students’ experiences with human- and artificial intelligence (AI)-based feedback. The empirical corpus consisted of 322 feedback-related reflection statements obtained from 110 undergraduate students. The analysis combined data preprocessing, corpus-driven thematic modeling with BERTopic, zero-shot thematic extraction using large language models (LLMs), ensemble-based semantic alignment, psycholinguistic emotion–theme integration, and high-resolution thematic refinement through a Mixture of Agents (MoA) framework. BERTopic identified six core themes: trust and transparency, cognitive load and clarity, learning contribution and perceived benefit, emotional discomfort and uncertainty, human-AI comparison, and complementary feedback expectations. The results showed that students’ feedback experiences were multidimensional, involving cognitive, affective, explanatory, and comparative dimensions rather than a simple preference for either feedback source. BERTopic provided a stable corpus-grounded thematic baseline, whereas Large Language Model (LLM)-based zero-shot extraction produced pedagogically interpretable and conceptually expressive theme labels. The ensemble approach reduced variation across individual LLM outputs by consolidating semantically similar labels. MoA further refined thematic distinctions and improved emotion–topic alignment, particularly in statements involving cognitive ambiguity or emotionally charged feedback experiences. Comparative analyses indicated that AI-based feedback was more strongly associated with speed, accessibility, consistency, and immediate learning support, whereas human feedback was more strongly associated with contextual richness, empathy, pedagogical explanation, and perceived authority. The findings suggest that effective feedback design should combine the scalability and immediacy of AI-based feedback with human oversight, contextual interpretation, emotional calibration, and transparent justification. Overall, the study contributes to learning analytics and feedback research by demonstrating how corpus-driven topic modeling, LLM-based interpretation, ensemble alignment, and MoA-based refinement can be integrated to model the cognitive and affective dimensions of students’ feedback experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: History-Aware Sequence Modeling for Authentic Learner Profiling in the Age of Generative AI
Source title: International Conference on Computer Supported Education, CSEDU - Proceedings
Affiliations: LIUM Computer Science Laboratory, University of Le Mans, Le Mans, France
Authors with affiliations: Ouared A., LIUM Computer Science Laboratory, University of Le Mans, Le Mans, France; May M., LIUM Computer Science Laboratory, University of Le Mans, Le Mans, France; Piau-Toffolon C., LIUM Computer Science Laboratory, University of Le Mans, Le Mans, France; Dugué N., LIUM Computer Science Laboratory, University of Le Mans, Le Mans, France
Abstract: Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot) enable students to delegate learning tasks, potentially obscuring authentic learning behaviors and the critical transition from declarative to procedural knowledge. Current learning analytics and AI detectors focus on coarse-grained outputs, failing to capture the nuanced dynamics of learning processes in generative AI-integrated contexts. However, identifying temporal GAI usage patterns such as passive profiles that seek generic help and copy answers, or active profiles that specify needs and target specific issues as well as the use of GAI for initial hints or scaffolding, remains challenging. We introduce Auth-LP (Authentic Learner Profiling), a history-aware sequence modeling framework that profiles authentic learning by analyzing timestamped event sequences (e.g., Prompted, AskGenAI, HelpSeeking, HintRequest, AcceptSugg, ReviseSugg, Modify) in educational contexts integrating generative AI. The framework captures task-level learner-AI assistant interactions and identifies behavioral states such as Engaged, Struggling, AI-Dependent, and Gaming the System. Auth-LP integrates visual analytics (e.g., heatmaps, radar charts) to monitor profile transitions as learners’ behavioral states evolve throughout the learning process. It enables educators to distinguish genuine skill development and learning agency from AI-assisted outputs, informing learning analytics design and enhancing personalized guidance. Our findings, based on a proof of concept conducted within the écri+ project, demonstrate that history-aware sequence modeling supports authentic learner profiling and trustworthy assessment, fostering Human-AI synergy for augmented learning in AI-augmented education. Title: AI-driven adaptive stealth assessment for socially regulated learning in collaborative environments

Authors with affiliations: Hadyaoui A., PRINCE Research Laboratory, Sousse University, ISITC, Hammam Sousse, Tunisia; Cheniti-Belcadhi L., PRINCE Research Laboratory, Sousse University, ISITC, Hammam Sousse, Tunisia
Abstract: Conventional digital assessments often overlook learners’ real-time progress, peer interactions, and cognitive demands. This study addresses these limitations by introducing GenSolve, an adaptive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven stealth assessment framework designed to adjust scenario complexity, deliver personalized feedback, and monitor group regulation using socially regulated learning (SoRL) principles. A six-week quasi-experimental study involving 250 undergraduates compared GenSolve to traditional instruction. Results showed a 17.6% gain in problem-solving accuracy, a 21% increase in group cohesion, and a 12.7% improvement in delayed retention. AI-generated feedback reduced repeated errors by 23.4% and improved self-regulation, while SoRL mechanisms supported a 36% rise in independent conflict resolution. GenSolve contributes a scalable, ethically guided model for real-time collaborative assessment, offering practical advances in adaptive evaluation for digital learning environments. © 2026 ISTE.

Abstract: This study developed and evaluated an AI-integrated Virtual Reality (VR) system designed to enhance personalized learning in higher education. While VR improves engagement, existing systems often lack adaptivity or experience high latency during AI interactions. To address these limitations, this research introduces a novel integration of a cache-optimized Llama 2 Large Language Model (LLM) that delivers real-time, motivationally grounded feedback. The system was implemented using Unity 3D and validated with 50 undergraduate students. Technical validation showed that the cache layer reduced interaction latency from 17.7 ms to 14.2 ms and maintained zero system crashes throughout the pilot. Learner motivation was assessed using Keller’s ARCS model, yielding mean scores ranging from 4.08 to 4.69 across all dimensions. Independent t-tests (p > 0.05) and negligible effect sizes (Cohen’s d < 0.2) revealed no significant difference between technical (ICT) and non-technical (Physics) students. These findings confirm that the proposed system effectively bridges technological and motivational gaps, providing a robust model for adaptive, immersive education. © 2025 by the authors.

Title: PRIVACY-ADAPTIVE GENERATIVE AI: FROM UNSTRUCTURED REPORTS TO COMPETENCY-BASED LEARNING ANALYTICS
Source title: Proceedings of the International CDIO Conference
Affiliations: Telecos-BCN, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC), Spain
Authors with affiliations: Garcia-Huertes S., Telecos-BCN, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC), Spain; Bragós R., Telecos-BCN, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC), Spain
Abstract: Background: Challenge-Based Learning (CBL) courses generate a wealth of unstructured student artifacts (e.g., reports, prototypes) that contain rich evidence of professional competencies (CDIO Standard 11). However, extracting these process variables for longitudinal analysis has historically required prohibitive manual effort, leaving valuable curriculum insights inaccessible. As a result, assessment practices often rely on coarse indicators (e.g., grades), limiting evidence-based feedback on innovation and professional skills. Challenge: While Generative AI offers a scalable solution to automate this extraction, institutions face a dilemma: utilizing frontier cloud models risks violating data sovereignty regulations, while privacy-preserving local models have historically lacked the reasoning capability required for complex assessment. Methodology: This paper presents a Privacy-Adaptive Dual-Pipeline framework to resolve this tension. We analyze a subset of 15-year archive of engineering capstone projects (N = 63 validated samples) by benchmarking a local, offline Large Language Model (LLM) against a frontier Cloud model. Results: We identify a distinct Inference Gap: while local models successfully extract explicit identity metadata (Title: 78.2% match), they struggle with semantic reasoning tasks (e.g., Value Proposition: 0.0% match) compared to the cloud benchmark. Contribution: We propose a tiered implementation strategy that allows educators to select the appropriate privacy tier based on data sensitivity. This methodology provides the CDIO community with a validated workflow to transform unstructured repositories into structured datasets, enabling scalable, evidence-based assessment and feedback without compromising student privacy. © 2026 22nd International CDIO Conference. Abstract: The process of associating elements of learning content with concepts or skills that this content helps students to master is one of the critical steps in developing personalized educational systems. When these associations are properly established, the system can infer the growth of student understanding of separate knowledge components from the logs of their interactions with associated learning content and use it to adapt the learning process accordingly by targeting gaps in individual students’ knowledge. Unfortunately, crafting these links between learning content and knowledge components is a very time- and expertise-demanding process that has traditionally been performed manually by domain experts with the help of knowledge engineers. Recently, the power of Large Language Models has motivated a new generation of research on concept extraction from textual learning content. The work presented in this paper contributes to this trend while introducing two important innovations. First, our concept extraction process is guided by a human-authored ontology of the target domain - Python programming. Second, alongside a traditional expert evaluation of the concept extraction quality, we apply two additional validation approaches: one based on using an educational data mining technique (learning curves) and another utilizing the pedagogical expertise of teaching the target domain (learning content placement). © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Blended Learning Design in Higher Education: A Systematic Review Through TPACK and AI Role Perspectives (2020–2025)
Source title: Education Sciences
Affiliations: School of Computing, Eastern Institute of Technology, Hawke’s Bay, Napier, 4112, New Zealand
Authors with affiliations: Dang D., School of Computing, Eastern Institute of Technology, Hawke’s Bay, Napier, 4112, New Zealand; Alani N.H.S., School of Computing, Eastern Institute of Technology, Hawke’s Bay, Napier, 4112, New Zealand; Nayani W., School of Computing, Eastern Institute of Technology, Hawke’s Bay, Napier, 4112, New Zealand; Erturk E., School of Computing, Eastern Institute of Technology, Hawke’s Bay, Napier, 4112, New Zealand
Abstract: This systematic literature review (SLR) examines the evolving nature of blended learning (BL) in higher education from 2020 to 2025. While BL is widely promoted for its flexibility, accessibility, and inclusivity, its practical application is uneven. This review integrated findings from 63 peer-reviewed studies obtained from five major academic databases and employed the PRISMA 2020 protocol to ensure methodological transparency and research quality. Findings were analysed using the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model and the AI Roles Framework to assess instructional design and technology integration. This analysis was conducted through a thematic approach to identify recurring patterns and key insights across the literature on BL and the use of emerging technologies such as AI, AR/VR, and learning analytics within BL. The study identifies three main challenges. There is an excessive application of tool-centric models such as TAM and UTAUT. Engagement with educators, administrators, and under-represented learners is limited. Ethical considerations related to the use of AI, AR/VR, and learning analytics are often overlooked. The most common issue is the higher dependence on models such as TAM and UTAUT. The review also shows that many educational applications reproduce similar design patterns and content structures, while insufficiently responding to learner diversity, digital readiness, accessibility needs, self-regulation capacity, and disciplinary context. While these models are helpful, they frequently limit complex teaching and learning environments to simple patterns of user behaviour. It is also clear that voices from teachers, support staff, and less-represented student groups are missing from the discussion. This is considered a serious concern because these technologies are increasingly being used in education. Moving forward, there is a clear need to shift away from rigid, technology-led models toward more adaptive, pedagogy-focused approaches. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of blended learning as an interconnected educational system. They also offer implications for future research, inclusive digital pedagogy, and policy development in higher education. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: The evolution of digital education tools has reshaped learning experiences, particularly for adult learners juggling diverse commitments. This study explores the transformative role of iSmartGuide, an AI-powered educational platform developed by the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), in addressing the unique needs of this demographic. By integrating cutting-edge technologies such as Generative AI (GenAI) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), iSmartGuide offers personalized, adaptive, and equitable learning experiences. The platform’s AI Tutor provides context-aware, tailored responses, enhancing student engagement and self-directed learning while equipping educators with actionable insights through advanced analytics. Features like mobile accessibility, interactive formats, and flexible personalization further support learners in navigating their educational journeys. This study examines the development, applications, and impact of iSmartGuide, highlighting its potential to set new benchmarks in lifelong learning and digital pedagogy. Future directions for AI in education and its implications for promoting accessibility and equity are also discussed, emphasizing the platform’s role in shaping the future of education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Longitudinal Shifts in Student Peer Feedback Before and During the GenAI Era
Source title: 2026 22nd International Conference on Information Technology Based Higher Education and Training, ITHET 2026
Affiliations: Johannes Kepler University, Institute Of Digital Business, Linz, Austria; Johannes Kepler University, Department Of Digital Education, Linz, Austria
Authors with affiliations: Stabauer M., Johannes Kepler University, Institute Of Digital Business, Linz, Austria; Katzlinger E., Johannes Kepler University, Department Of Digital Education, Linz, Austria
Abstract: Peer review is widely used to scale formative assessment and develop feedback literacy, yet evidence about how student peer feedback evolves over multiple cohorts remains scarce. This paper analyzes a longitudinal corpus of anonymized peer reviews on seminar papers collected across eight annual cohorts (2019-2026). Each student reviewed three peers using a rubric with criterion-level ratings and open comments, plus an overall assessment. We quantify changes in the discourse of peer feedback using reproducible text-based measures (verbosity, lexical diversity, rhetorical markers) and relate these to rating severity and review timing. To examine shifts plausibly associated with widespread adoption of generative AI tools following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, we compare a pre-period (2019-2022) with a post-period (2024-2026), treating 2023 as a transition year. Results show a marked increase in criterion-comment length after 2024 (+54% words), a concurrent decrease in lexical diversity, and a rise in summary/conclusion markers (e.g., "insgesamt", "Fazit"). At the same time, criterion grades become slightly more critical. We discuss these shifts as signatures of changing peer-feedback practices in a GenAI era and derive design implications for preserving authenticity and learning value in rubric-based peer assessment.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Applications on University Teaching Quality and Students’ Self-Directed Learning Skills
Source title: Social Science Forum
Affiliations: Department of Basic Sciences and Humanities, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Amman Arab University, Amman, Jordan
Authors with affiliations: Al-Otaibi M., Department of Basic Sciences and Humanities, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Amman Arab University, Amman, Jordan
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications are rapidly reshaping university teaching through adaptive tutoring, generative dialogue, automated feedback, learning analytics, predictive support, and AI-assisted assessment. Yet the educational value of these applications depends not merely on access to technology but on how they are embedded in pedagogy. This study examines the impact of AI applications on university teaching quality and students’ self-directed and self-regulated learning skills. It uses a systematic integrative review and a secondary quantitative synthesis of verified, peer-reviewed evidence. The principal quantitative corpus comprises 85 higher-education studies, 387 dependent effect-size estimates, and 9,564 participants published between 2015 and 2025. Descriptive analyses were reconstructed from publicly available supplementary data, while inferential conclusions were based on published three-level and random-effects meta-analytic estimates; no synthetic data were used. AI feedback had a medium positive average effect on self-regulated learning (Hedges’ g = 0.509), but its 95% prediction interval ranged from −0.661 to 1.678, indicating that effects are highly conditional. Generative-AI interventions also improved academic performance (g = 0.683, 95% CI [0.17, 1.19]), while ChatGPT-supported learning improved behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement. However, heterogeneity was substantial, AI feedback did not clearly outperform human feedback, and experimental evidence identified risks of dependence, shallow processing, and “metacognitive laziness.” Teacher support emerged as a decisive pedagogical condition in the academic-performance literature: teacher-supported student–AI interaction produced a large effect (g = 1.426), whereas unsupported use produced a near-zero effect (g = 0.077). The study concludes that AI can improve university teaching quality and learner autonomy when it functions as a scaffold within teacher-designed learning, not as a substitute for disciplinary teaching, human feedback, reflective judgment, or independent performance. © 2026 Slovenian Sociological Association. Title: Design and Implementation of an AI Integrated Educational Assistant for Learning
Source title: SN Computer Science
Affiliations: Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India
Authors with affiliations: Jothikumar K., Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India; Velusamy G., Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India; Meenakshi A.J., Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India; Aruna Varshini S., Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India; Anisha S., Computer Science and Engineering, National Engineering College, Tamilnadu, Kovilpatti, India
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are transforming higher education by enabling data-driven personalization, adaptive assessment, and informed instructional decision-making. Conventional learning management systems (LMSs) primarily support content delivery but lack mechanisms for providing actionable insights to educators or personalized guidance to learners. To address these limitations, this study introduces an AI-Supported Learning Analytics Platform that integrates three key functions: (i) personalized learner support through intelligent matching and recommendations, (ii) automated quiz generation and evaluation using large language models, and (iii) conversational assistance for real-time interaction. The platform not only enhances student engagement but also collects interaction and performance data, which are trans- formed into analytics for educators to inform course design and pedagogical strategies. A mixed-method research design, combining system development with quasi-experimental evaluation, was employed in a higher education context. Findings indicate that students using the proposed platform achieved higher academic performance, greater engagement, and improved satisfaction compared to those using traditional LMSs. Moreover, the analytics generated provided educators with valuable feedback for evidence-based decision-making. This study contributes to the field of educational technology by (1) demonstrating how AI- driven personalization, assessment, and conversational support can be embedded in higher education platforms, (2) highlighting the role of learning analytics in supporting both student learning and educator decision-making, and (3) offering a framework for integrating AI-supported analytics into institutional teaching and learning practices. The results affirm the potential of AI-enhanced systems to strengthen both learner experiences and institutional decision-making in higher education. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Effective peer feedback is essential for developing critical reflection in higher education, yet its impact is often limited by the inconsistent quality of student-generated comments. This paper presents the implementation and deployment of AICoFe (AI-based Collaborative Feedback), a system designed to bridge this gap through a human-centered AI approach. We describe a modular architecture that orchestrates a multi-LLM pipeline—utilizing GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Llama 3.1—to synthesize quantitative rubric data and qualitative observations into coherent, actionable feedback. Key to the system is a”teacher-in-the-loop” mediation workflow, where educators use specialized Learning Analytics dashboards to curate and refine AI-generated drafts before delivery. Furthermore, we detail the underlying data infrastructure, which employs a hybrid SQL and MongoDB strategy to ensure traceability and manage semi-structured feedback versions. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMS) generate rich activity and interaction logs that can be exploited using machine learning techniques. This study models temporal engagement patterns, such as early, middle, late, weekend, and night activity, derived from Moodle logs in multiple undergraduate courses. It constructs temporal feature vectors per-student, applies k-means clustering to uncover behavioral patterns, and then uses ANOVA and Kruskal–Wallis tests to assess whether patterns differ in final grades. Results show that the predictive value of temporal patterns is highly course-dependent; in some courses, structured early engagement aligns with higher achievement, whereas in others, heavy weekend and night usage is associated with the best outcomes. To complement the obtained quantitative analyses, a Large Language Model (LLM) (i.e., ChatGPT) is evaluated as a zero-shot classifier that receives only natural-language summaries of temporal behavior and predicts performance tiers. While accuracy is limited, the model produces a coherent approach, indicating value as an interpretable layer on top of statistical analysis. The work demonstrates a generalizable pipeline for temporal feature engineering, unsupervised profiling, and LLM-based reasoning over LMS data for early risk detection in digital learning environments. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: Fostering engagement among undergraduate computer science students in large-lecture settings can be challenging for instructors. Didactic teaching styles common in such lectures may not be as effective as dialogic teaching, but the overhead involved with dialogic teaching may preclude its use in large introductory computer science courses. Classroom response systems such as multiple-choice “clicker” systems provide a way for students to engage with an instructor, but evidence suggests that multiple-choice questions may not foster deep thought in the way that open-ended questions do. Open-ended questions foster deeper engagement and AI-enabled learning analytics offer a powerful method of automatically assessing student responses, but grading text responses produced by students and summarizing class-wide performance during lectures presents unique difficulties, especially for algorithmic questions prevalent in computer science lectures. We present a system for delivering, assessing, and summarizing students’ responses to open-ended question prompts during such lectures. A central part of this system is the effective summarization of topic-level student responses to provide actionable feedback to the instructor. This poster presents an early phase of this summarization work, analyzing both the quantitative semantic accuracy and qualitative usefulness to instructors of an LLM-based system that summarizes student feedback. Semantic accuracy is found to be high and consistent across different summarization methods. Instructor interviews identified several key qualities of summaries that would be useful, including format preferences and features that would allow selective insight into student responses related to misconceptions. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: While AI literacy frameworks are becoming more widely adopted, a key gap remains: we still lack practical infrastructure for educators to collect, share, and understand real classroom cases that connect framework ideas to situated teaching practice. Such infrastructure may help strengthen the connection between theory and practice. In this work, we present AILitHub, a multilingual and scalable web system that enables teachers to contribute AI-related educational cases and annotate them with stakeholders and competencies defined in the OECD AI Literacy Framework. We position AILitHub as an early infrastructure for future professional learning and research. It contributes a scalable case-collection mechanism and may provide practice-grounded evidence that can inform future framework refinement and AI education design. In a preliminary deployment within an AI literacy professional training program, we successfully collected 53 complete teacher-contributed cases. Early results suggest that, while teachers showed strength in contributing positive cases demonstrating AI literacy, they may lack the skill or awareness to identify and provide negative examples. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Title: Adversarial Assignment Perturbation: Effects on Help-Seeking Behaviors in Student Generative AI Chatbot Use
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: North Carolina State University, Raleigh, United States
Authors with affiliations: Gilson S., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, United States; Tabarsi B., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, United States; Barnes T., North Carolina State University, Raleigh, United States
Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI (GenAI) tools in educational settings necessitates methods to differentiate student-AI interactions indicative of productive help-seeking from shallow cognitive outsourcing. This work conducts a mixed-methods analysis of GenAI queries and learning in an undergraduate discrete mathematics course. Participants were provided with an optional, GenAI-powered chatbot to aid them while completing a One-Shot GenAI-Resistant assignment, generated via an iterative perturbation process. We conducted a case study of 8 students who used the chatbot, and found two disparate engagement patterns: cognitive scaffolding, recongizing GenAI chatbot had hallucinated and provided additional context to leverage the chatbot to discover the correct answer, and GenAI dependence behaviors, which failed to critically evaluate hallucinated GenAI chatbot answers. Within this small sample, we found a significant correlation between cognitive scaffolding and GenAI dependent engagement patterns and the perturbed assignment grades. These findings demonstrate that assignment perturbation, combined with chat log analysis, can be used to differentiate deep and shallow GenAI engagement strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Outcome-Based Assessment (OBA) has become a core requirement in higher education quality assurance because it links curriculum design, assessment evidence, attainment analysis, and continuous quality improvement to measurable student outcomes. In practice, however, OBA is still frequently managed through spreadsheets, disconnected tools, and manual reporting, which weaken traceability and increase administrative burden. Therefore, this paper proposes EduTrack, a centralized Outcome-Based Assessment Management System, designed to operationalize the OBA lifecycle in a single platform. EduTrack supports structured outcome management across the outcome-based mapping hierarchy, assessment planning, rubric-based score processing, role-based access control, evidence management, dashboard-based reporting, and support for continuous improvement. The platform is implemented as an on-premise containerized system using Next.js, NestJS, PostgreSQL, Metabase, Python analytical services, and optional local language model integration through Ollama. Compared with prior OBA frameworks and representative systems, EduTrack emphasizes three differentiators: integrated multi-level traceability from program outcomes to course evidence, combined direct and indirect evidence workflows in one system, and an AI-assisted module whose evaluation pipeline calibrates judge models against human annotations before downstream use. As a result, EduTrack provides a practical, auditable, and extensible foundation for institution-scale OBA management while keeping AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance controlled and accountable.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Detecting Doubt in Reflective Learning: A Learning Analytics Study with Large and Small Language Models
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore
Authors with affiliations: Ouh E.L., Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore; Tan K.W., Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore; Lo S.L., Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore; Zhang Y., Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore
Abstract: Reflective learning enhances understanding, especially when instructors promptly address difficulties raised in student reflections. Automated doubt detection can reduce time for instructors, yet existing classification approaches take substantial time for manual annotation and model training. This paper investigates whether large and small language models (LLMs, SLMs) can automate doubt detection without time-consuming training. Using a dataset of anonymized student reflections, we evaluate zero-shot, few-shot prompting, and multi-step reasoning against prior supervised classification baselines. We show that LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude-4, Gemini-2.5) surpass earlier F1 scores without prompting, while prompting further improves their performance. However, using proprietary LLMs can raise cost and privacy concerns. We also show that selected SLMs (Mistral, Qwen) outperform baselines while addressing these concerns. We extend the analysis with a category-level error study, showing that explicit doubts are detected more reliably, while tentative doubts (softened by cautious language), learning challenge (arising from difficulties in applying concepts), and masked doubts (concealed by positive or polite phrasing) are missed more often. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of language models for doubt detection and the need to ensure that cautious or polite learners who may not express their doubts explicitly are recognized and supported in learning analytics systems. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Fact-Check-Game for Cognitive Defense: Log-Based Evidence and Pedagogical Design Implications for AI-Age Information Literacy
Source title: 2026 14th International Conference on Information and Education Technology, ICIET 2026
Affiliations: Institute of Arts and Sciences, Yamagata University, Yamagata, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Kanoh H., Institute of Arts and Sciences, Yamagata University, Yamagata, Japan
Abstract: Misinformation risks have intensified with the spread of social media and generative AI, increasing the need for repeated practice of fact-checking as a behavioral skill. This study designed, implemented, and deployed Fact-Check-Game; a lightweight Share/Verify/Skip serious game built with Google Apps Script and Google Sheets to support classroom practice and log-based learning analytics. In a classroom deployment (n = 6 5 sessions; 553 completed trials), Verify was used in only 42/553 trials (7.6%), while false sharing persisted (20 553,3.6% of completed trials). Theme-wise analyses suggested that verification behavior varied by topic, and reaction time distributions indicated greater cognitive effort when learners engaged in verification. We discuss pedagogical implications for teaching fact-checking as cognitive defense and provide design recommendations to better align incentives and scaffolding with verification habits in the AIage.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Comparing human and LLM ordered coding of qualitative data: How coding differences cascade through temporal analysis
Source title: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Center of Advanced Technology for Assisted Learning and Predictive Analytics (CATALPA), FernUniversität in Hagen, Germany; School of Computing, University of Eastern Finland, Joensuu, Finland; School of Computing and Information Systems, University of Melbourne, Australia; University of Wisconsin-Madison, United States

Abstract: Automating the process of qualitatively coding text data from learners has been a long-standing ambition of learning analytics researchers since it represents an essential step toward delivering timely and scalable feedback. Automating this process is especially challenging in the case of ordered coding schemes —necessary for temporal analytical methods— where one text utterance can be assigned more than one qualitative code and the assignment order matters. This problem goes beyond multi-class and multi-label classification and, therefore, cannot be easily tackled using classic language models such as BERT. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, especially with the advent of large language models, have —allegedly— created a substantial step forward in making the goal of automatically coding complex temporal data attainable. However, little is yet known about how to implement this process in a way that most closely resembles human coding, i.e., taking into account the context in which the textual data appears for accurate interpretation. Moreover, due to the complexity of the data and its shape, the accuracy of the results cannot be computed using classic accuracy metrics. This study makes two main contributions: first, it presents two evaluation approaches for assessing the quality of ordered data coding and the usability of LLM in automatically coding ordered processes; and second, it demonstrates a method of LLM prompting that leverages a consistent context window. Our results reveal systematic and statistically significant differences between LLM and human coding across structural, transitional, and code-level metrics for binary and ordered tasks. As classification errors can propagate through automated feedback systems, relying on LLM outputs risks amplifying inaccuracies and producing misleading interpretations of learning processes. © 2026 The Authors.

Affiliations: Computer Science, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines; Information Technology, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines
Authors with affiliations: Arguson A.C., Computer Science, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines; Ambat S.C., Computer Science, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines; Malasaga E.V., Computer Science, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines; Ramos R.F., Information Technology, FEU Institute of Technology, Sampaloc, Manila, Philippines
Abstract: The proposed research aims to develop a hybrid learning analytics model that incorporates clickstream and sentiment mining techniques to accurately predict student retention in Learning Management Systems (LMS) in Manila-based HEIs. This proposed research aims to improve the limitations of single prediction modeling. The proposed research utilized a quantitative explanatory research design and was applied to undergraduate students taking general education courses. The proposed research utilized stratified sampling to select a total of 345 students. Clickstream and text-based interaction data were analyzed to obtain sequence and sentiment-based metrics to train the hybrid prediction model using Logistic Regression and XGBoost. The engagement tool was also able to reach Cronbach's alpha = 0.91, which is a good measure of internal consistency. This shows that the click-only model had an AUC of 0.78, but the hybrid model was enhanced to 0.84, with the top predictors being attempts at quizzes per week and negative sentiment ratio. This shows the importance of multimodal analytics in the improvement of early warning systems and proactive interventions. The implication of this can be seen in the administration of the institution and the academic support, which is a basis for evidence-based retention and fairness-based predictive models in Philippine Higher Education.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Standard learning provenance taxonomy (SLPT): An open specification and JSON schema for learner–AI interaction records
Source title: SoftwareX
Affiliations: Center for International Security and Cooperation, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Answer Labs Inc., Newark, DE, United States; Division of Operations and Information Management, Babson College, Wellesley, MA, United States; Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, United States

Abstract: The purpose of this paper is to define a portable format for recording how learners interact with generative AI. The Standard Learning Provenance Taxonomy (SLPT) is an open specification and JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) for Learning Provenance Records, defining four first-order interaction dimensions and one candidate composite, six context-filter criteria, an episode-level delegation annotation, and a conformance surface. Schema validation demonstrates conformance: a corpus of 71 fixtures, 17 positive and 54 negative, reproduces its expected outcome in every case. It does not establish that interaction traces validly measure cognition, and it does not demonstrate interoperability across independent implementations, which would require multi-implementation exchange testing not attempted here. SLPT records the provenance of an interaction, not of a learner's knowledge, and restricts current score use to formative and research contexts. We conclude that the contribution is a record-and-conformance layer, not a validated assessment instrument. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: Analyzing the complex dialogue central to computer-supported collaborative learning is crucial for understanding learning processes, yet remains a significant challenge for educational researchers due to the labor-intensive nature of manual coding and the semantic limitations of traditional computational methods. Recent advancements have highlighted the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to move beyond mere automation, demonstrating an ability for inference without task-specific data that is characteristic of artificial general intelligence. To harness this potential, this study introduced and evaluated a human-AI collaborative framework (CGT-LLM) that integrates LLMs into computational grounded theory. Specifically, CGT-LLM focuses on learning analytics for rich discursive data. Applied to dialogue from a climate change collaborative simulation game, the framework was evaluated against a supervised bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT) baseline. The performance of the framework approached human expert-level performance in categories related to explicit instructions, numerical data, or direct statements of intent crucial to game objectives, while also demonstrating promising capability in identifying more abstract and less obvious themes. The findings demonstrate that the researcher's role in computational grounded theory remains critical, particularly in exploring data diversity during the discovery phase, and making final interpretive judgments for abstract themes during the classification phase. This framework thus positions LLMs as a valuable assistant rather than as a replacement for human expertise, providing educators and researchers with a tool to gain deeper, more scalable insights into collaborative learning processes, and offering potential to inform the design of timely pedagogical interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: As higher education increasingly relies on data-driven decision-making, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict student success and dropout rates is gaining further importance. The primary aim of this study is to understand the evolutionary research trends of data-driven student success management. A PRISMA-based bibliometric analysis of 457 articles is implemented using the R software version 4.5.3 and the bibliometrix package (Version 5.0). Published articles are retrieved from Web of Science Core Collection indexes (SSCI, AHCI, ESCI), covering a three-decade period (1996-2025). The rigorous inclusion/exclusion criteria restricted the dataset to English-language, and peer-reviewed journal articles. Furthermore, co-word analysis and conceptual structure mapping, utilizing the Louvain clustering algorithm, were applied to extract the thematic architecture of the domain. Performance analysis reveals China and U.S. universities as the most influential affiliations shaping the structural volume of this research field, with Applied Sciences emerging as the dominant journal. Additionally, the network analysis indicates an international collaboration rate of 25%. The thematic map reveals that while predictive modeling-based Early Warning Systems (EWS) have matured into Basic Themes, driving Motor Themes included generative artificial intelligence and psychological constructs. Furthermore, Emerging Themes show that explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is drawing a transformative pathway to the field. Higher education managers should integrate XAI while addressing ethical AI governance. Future higher education data-driven management should focus on building transparent systems leading to the empowerment of human decision-makers. © 2026, Qubahan. All rights reserved.

Title: Design and Evaluation of an AI-Supported Automated Programming Assessment Environment for Concept-Aligned Reinforcement in Engineering and Computing Education
Source title: Computer Applications in Engineering Education
Affiliations: Department of Information Management, National Formosa University, Yunlin County, Huwei Township, Taiwan
Authors with affiliations: Lan Y.-F., Department of Information Management, National Formosa University, Yunlin County, Huwei Township, Taiwan
Abstract: Automated programming assessment systems are widely used in engineering and computing education to support scalable programming practice, but correctness-based verdicts often provide limited concept-level reinforcement for novice learners. This study designed and evaluated an AI-supported automated programming assessment environment that transforms verified incorrect submissions into governed, concept-aligned micro-assessments. Rather than using generative AI as an open-ended tutor or grading agent, the proposed environment used AI as a constrained orchestration layer within a deterministic assessment workflow. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was implemented in an introductory Python programming course with 90 first-year undergraduate students, including 45 students in the experimental group and 45 students in the control group. Both groups completed the same macro-level programming tasks through the same automated assessment system, whereas the experimental group additionally received assessment-triggered, learner-initiated micro-assessment opportunities through a mobile chatbot after verified incorrect submissions. Results indicated that learners in the experimental group demonstrated higher post-intervention concept-level mastery across all five programming components and reported greater gains in programming self-efficacy and higher post-intervention learning motivation. Log-based analyses further showed sustained engagement with the reinforcement environment, with learners completing an average of 51.3 micro-assessment interactions and 46% of these interactions occurring outside class sessions. These findings suggest that a governed, evidence-anchored reinforcement workflow can extend automated programming assessment systems from correctness evaluation toward scalable, concept-aligned support, although the observed advantages should be interpreted as outcomes associated with the integrated environment rather than as isolated effects of generative AI or additional practice alone. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.

Abstract: This study reviewed 50 years of research on technology-enhanced science and mathematics education published in Computers & Education (1976–2026). Following PRISMA 2020 framework, 519 empirical studies were identified. BERTopic-based topic modeling was applied to derive the thematic structure of the corpus, and each article was coded for education level, theoretical framework, primary technology, and technology function. Seventeen topics were identified, including ten science-related, four mathematics-related, and three domain-general ones. Topic membership was more strongly associated with primary technology and technology function than with education level and theoretical framework. Game-based learning split into separate science and mathematics topics, and a mathematics-centered AI/agent topic emerged, while AI-related science studies were found to be mainly assigned to existing topics such as argumentation, collaborative learning, and inquiry. VR was a distinct technological topic and served several instructional functions. Besides, research within this corpus shifted from computer-centered instructional agendas toward a more diverse space encompassing learning analytics, games, mobile and immersive environments, eye tracking, and AI, with integrated STEM and eye-tracking topics emerging in this corpus around the mid-2010s. Science-related work differentiated around disciplinary practices, whereas mathematics-related work clustered around forms of instructional support rather than mathematical subdomains. Future work can extend the BERTopic framework to a broader set of journals to fully understand the overall trends, or apply BERTopic method separately to publications within fixed intervals to examine how research topics evolve over time. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Personalized AI Practice Replicates Learning Rate Regularity at Scale
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Campus AI, New York, United States
Authors with affiliations: Beauchesne J., Campus AI, New York, United States; Maroti C., Campus AI, New York, United States; Bratman J., Campus AI, New York, United States; Pesenti J., Campus AI, New York, United States; Holt L., Campus AI, New York, United States; Tambellini A., Campus AI, New York, United States; McGrath A., Campus AI, New York, United States; Guo M., Campus AI, New York, United States; Peterson S., Campus AI, New York, United States
Abstract: Recent research demonstrated that students exhibit consistent learning rates across diverse educational contexts. We test these findings using a dataset of 1.8 million (366k post-filtering) student interactions from the digital platform Campus AI providing further evidence for the observation of regularity in learning rate among students. Unlike prior work requiring manual cognitive modeling, Campus AI automatically generates Knowledge Components (KCs) and corresponding exercises, both of which are validated by human experts. This one-to-many mapping facilitates the application of Additive Factors Models to measure learning parameters without complex cognitive modeling. Using mixed-effects logistic regression, we confirmed the core finding of prior work: students displayed substantial variation in initial knowledge (IQR=[2.78,12.18] practice opportunities to reach 80% mastery) but remarkably consistent learning rates (IQR=[7.01,8.25] opportunities). Furthermore, students using this fully automated system achieved 80% mastery in a median of 7.22 practice opportunities, comparable to the 6.54 reported for expert-designed curricula. These results suggest that automated, science-grounded content generation can produce learning signatures comparable to expert-designed systems at scale. Data and code are publicly available (https://github.com/Campus-edu-AI/learning-rate). © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Students’ engagement with generative AI in academic learning: A self-determination theory and epistemic network analysis study
Source title: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence
Affiliations: Khazar University, Baku, Azerbaijan; Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey; Mapua University, Manila, Philippines; Ozyegin University, Istanbul, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Isaeva R., Khazar University, Baku, Azerbaijan; Caner H.N., Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey; Caner M., Akdeniz University, Antalya, Turkey; Giray L., Mapua University, Manila, Philippines; Karadag E., Ozyegin University, Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract: This qualitative case study examines undergraduate students' engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic learning in an English-medium university setting. This study employs self-determination theory (SDT) as the primary interpretive framework, treating technology acceptance perceptions (e.g., usefulness and ease of use) as descriptive cues rather than explanatory constructs. Data from 23 semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, complemented by epistemic network analysis (ENA) to examine the structural relationships among themes in students' discourse, with automated coding validated against a manually coded subset. Students frequently described GenAI as supporting efficiency and conceptual understanding; however, their accounts revealed persistent tensions concerning creativity, trust, and academic integrity. The ENA results showed that these concerns were systematically interconnected: discussions of learning support consistently co-occurred with verification practices, reflecting a “trust-but-verify” repertoire through which students calibrated their reliance on AI while maintaining epistemic control. Beyond instrumental evaluations, students' narratives highlighted broader value- and norm-related considerations, including algorithmic bias, environmental sustainability, and the positioning of AI within human–teacher learning networks. Overall, the findings suggest that students' engagement with GenAI is best understood as a motivated and socially situated learning practice shaped by the negotiation of competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Pedagogically, the results support a shift from prohibition-oriented responses to transparent institutional guidance, autonomy-supportive scaffolding of verification practices and AI literacy, and process-oriented assessment designs that make students' reasoning visible. Learning analytics approaches, such as ENA, may further assist educators in examining how these practices become integrated into students’ learning processes. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Unpacking the impact mechanism of generative AI-based learning analytics technology on student learning engagement: the mediating role of community of inquiry and the moderating role of digital literacy
Source title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Xi’an Shiyou University, Xi’an, 710065, China; Teachers College for Vocational and Technical Education, Nanning Normal University, Nanning, 530001, China; China-ASEAN Vocational Education Research Center, Nanning Normal University, Nanning, 530001, China; School of Mathematics and Physics, Yibin University, Yibin, 644000, China

Abstract: This study investigates how generative AI-based learning analytics technology (GLAT) influences university students’ learning engagement through the mediating role of the Community of Inquiry (CoI), and how digital literacy moderates this relationship. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) and CoI framework, the research explores the mechanism through which intelligent learning resources are transformed into learning behaviors, complementing classic learning theories with a unified “resource-capability-performance” analytical framework. Employing a mixed-methods design, data were collected through a two-phase survey (n = 400) and semi-structured interviews (n = 12). Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were used to systematically examine the relationships among GLAT, the three dimensions of CoI (cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence), digital literacy, and learning engagement. The findings reveal that: (1) GLAT has a significant direct effect on learning engagement; (2) the three dimensions of CoI partially mediate the relationship between GLAT and learning engagement; (3) digital literacy positively moderates the effect of GLAT on each CoI dimension; (4) digital literacy positively moderates the direct effect of GLAT on learning engagement; and (5) fsQCA identifies four sufficient configurations leading to high learning engagement, highlighting a multifaceted mechanism encompassing technology, interaction, and capability. This study enriches the application of RBV and CoI in intelligent learning environments and offers theoretical and practical implications for enhancing GLAT design and student support strategies in higher education. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Assessing Student Satisfaction and Reuse Intention through Predictive Modeling of AI Assistant Interaction Data
Source title: Proceedings of 3rd International Conference on Machine Learning and Autonomous Systems, ICMLAS 2026
Affiliations: North Eastern Mindanao State University, Computer Science Department, Surigao del Sur, Tagbina, Philippines; College of Compuitng and Information Sciences, Agusan Del Sur State College of Agriculture and Technology, Bunawan, Philippines

Abstract: This The increasing adoption of AI-powered assistants such as ChatGPT in higher education has reshaped how students perform academic tasks, creating a growing need to understand the behavioral factors that drive satisfaction and continued use. This study proposes a predictive modeling approach to assess student satisfaction and reuse intention based exclusively on AI assistant interaction data. A dataset comprising 10,000 AI-assisted learning sessions was analyzed, incorporating behavioral and contextual features such as session duration, number of prompts, task type, perceived assistance level, and learning outcomes. Following data preprocessing and feature engineering, XGBoost classifier was implemented to model reuse intention and identify key predictors of satisfaction. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 0.92, demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing non-linear relationships within student-AI interaction data. Results reveal that longer interaction sessions, higher prompt frequencies, and greater perceived assistance levels are strongly associated with increased satisfaction and higher likelihood of reuse. Moreover, cognitively demanding tasks such as writing and coding exhibited higher satisfaction ratings compared to routine academic tasks. The findings highlight the potential of machine learning-based predictive modeling as a data-driven approach for understanding student engagement with AI assistants, offering actionable insights for educators and system designers to enhance AI-supported learning environments and foster sustained student engagement. © 2026 IEEE.

Author full names: Wang, Wei (58951642100); Pritchard, Cody (59415060100); Rosenberg, Joshua (56735393600)
Title: Analyzing Educational Video Transcripts with LLMs: Accuracy, Named Entities, and Interpretability
Source title: Journal of Educational Data Mining
Affiliations: University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States
Authors with affiliations: Wang W., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States; Pritchard C., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States; Rosenberg J., University of Tennessee Knoxville, United States
Abstract: Digital educational media platforms such as YouTube are increasingly used by teachers and learners, creating a growing record of instructional discourse. For educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics researchers, transcript-derived text offers a scalable entry point for corpus-level analysis, but automatically generated transcripts can contain errors that disproportionately affect named entities and downstream applications. We report an initial validation study of a transcript-to-entity workflow for educational video analysis. The workflow benchmarks multiple automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, evaluates GPT-4o and GPT-5.5 against a 600-token human consensus named-entity benchmark, compares both LLMs with an off-the-shelf spaCy transformer NER pipeline, and applies the model best aligned with the study-specific coding frame to a 48-episode corpus from the Crash Course U.S. History series. The results reveal an important task-dependent trade-off: spaCy performed best at general entity detection, whereas GPT-5.5 showed stronger aggregate performance for codebook-constrained entity typing on gold-entity rows. This finding supports the use of GPT-5.5 for the study’s type-specific corpus profiling without implying universal model superiority. Across the full corpus, PERSON, GPE, and NORP were the most frequent model-coded categories. Topic modeling comparisons further show that transcript-conditioning choices can change thematic separation and interpretability. Together, the findings demonstrate why transcript quality and entity validity should be evaluated according to the downstream educational research task. The workflow provides a reproducible starting point whose corpus-scale outputs can support navigation, sampling, and targeted human review rather than definitive annotation. © 2026 International Educational Data Mining Society. Abstract: The rapid emergence of Generative AI (GenAI), which gained momentum following the introduction of transformer architecture by Vaswani et al. (2017), has expanded the scope of what learning analytics (LA) can achieve. Traditional approaches to LA have emphasized the importance of understanding learners and their surrounding contexts (Ferguson, 2012). Yet in an increasingly AI-mediated world, there is a growing need to examine not only learners themselves, but the dynamic context of student-AI interactions (Noy & Zhang, 2023). Insights about how students appropriate, resist, or adapt to GenAI-based agents are integral to their continued learning process, particularly as we see the GenAI become increasingly integrated into educational tools such as intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) (Schmucker et al., 2023). Consequently, this opens an opportunity for LA to evolve beyond tracking traditional learning behaviors, toward analyzing how students seek support and construct meaning through interactions with GenAI-driven ITS. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Mohd Anas Wajid and Claudia Camacho-Zuñiga; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Agentic AI Orchestrators for Real-Time Learner Support in Low - Resource Open and Distance Learning: A Framework Grounded in Multi-Agent and Edge AI Literature
Source title: Innovations and Challenges of Agentic AI and Intelligent Agents in Education
Affiliations: She and Tech Empowerment Foundation, Abuja, Nigeria
Authors with affiliations: Adewale M.D., She and Tech Empowerment Foundation, Abuja, Nigeria; Sambo-Magaji A., She and Tech Empowerment Foundation, Abuja, Nigeria
Abstract: Open and distance learning (ODL) serves cohorts of learners under fragile connectivity, yet most early warning and learning analytics tools remain batch, central dashboards that rely on human interpretation and escalation instead of autonomous support. In parallel, work on agentic artificial intelligence (AAI), multi-agent systems (MAS), and edge to cloud computing has produced architectures for perception, decision making and control in domains. This chapter proposes a conceptual framework that transfers these design patterns to low-resource ODL by treating the ecosystem as a multilayer agentic environment with three core classes of agents: learner support agents at the edge, course and programme orchestrator agents at institutional layers, and governance and ethics agents that encode privacy, fairness and accountability while supervising autonomous control loops. We specify agent roles, data and model flows and oversight mechanisms, and use scenarios such as exam periods and connectivity disruptions to outline implications for designing transparent agentic AI in ODL. Abstract: Reflection is essential in healthcare education as it allows nursing students to assess their knowledge, skills, and understanding of learning material. Simulations allow students to build clinical and soft skills by reflecting on their decision-making and actions. Learning analytics (LA) dashboards can support reflection on simulation experiences by visualising multimodal data. However, the effectiveness of this information is limited by students’ ability to comprehend the data and derive actionable insights to improve their practice. Generative AI (GenAI) may address this challenge by providing simplified explanations of data, but little is known about how GenAI interventions (e.g., chatbots or AI-generated summaries) support reflections on LA data. To address this gap, we designed a LA dashboard augmented with either a chatbot or AI-generated summary to be used as a support tool by nursing students to reflect on clinical simulation experiences. Preliminary results show that AI-summaries lead nursing students to discuss plans of future actions in their written reflections, while chatbot-supported reflections tend to engage in self-assessment in addition to future planning and discussion of insights from the simulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Affiliations: School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China; Key Laboratory of Education Informatization for Nationalities of Ministry of Education, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiao S., School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China, Key Laboratory of Education Informatization for Nationalities of Ministry of Education, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China; Yang Z., School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China, Key Laboratory of Education Informatization for Nationalities of Ministry of Education, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China; Li S., Key Laboratory of Education Informatization for Nationalities of Ministry of Education, Yunnan Normal University, Kunming, China
Abstract: Artificial intelligence supports feedback, diagnosis, prediction, intervention, and scoring in online learning, yet technical performance alone does not establish how an AI-generated output should be interpreted or used as assessment evidence. This systematic scoping review and evidence map examined computational approaches, assessment-use impact, publication-language patterns, and technical validation evidence in Chinese- and English-language reports published from 1 January 2020 to 31 May 2026. The search programme covered 13 structured information sources, supplemented by additional retrieval and citation tracking. Retained search and export records documented at least 7, 969 retrieval/export occurrences before source-level relevance filtering and cross-source consolidation. After consolidation, 436 identifiable candidate report instances entered report-level reconciliation; one residual exact duplicate was removed, leaving 435 unique reports for eligibility assessment. Of these, 378 were included and 57 excluded. The individual report (publication) was the unit of analysis. Among the included reports, 99 were Chinese-language (26.2%) and 279 English-language (73.8%). Classical machine learning/data mining, deep learning/neural models, and learning analytics/statistical modeling together accounted for 68.3% of the evidence base. Assessment-use impact was concentrated in decision-support applications: 45 reports (11.9%) were Low impact, 323 (85.4%) Medium impact, and 10 (2.6%) High impact. LLM/generative AI accounted for six reports (1.6%). A focused technical subset of 15 High-impact and/or LLM/generative AI reports underwent task-specific performance synthesis and seven-domain technical validation appraisal. Eleven reports contained sufficient evidence for scoring (three Substantial, six Moderate, and two Limited), while four remained source-limited and unscored. Several reports documented strong task-specific performance or human–machine agreement, but no independent external validation was identified in the available evidence for the focused subset. Overall, the literature is dominated by Medium-impact diagnostic and decision-support uses. Task-level performance, internal validation, and cross-context generalizability represent distinct layers of evidence, supporting a use-sensitive approach to assessment-use calibration. © 2026 Jiao, Yang and Li.
