Title: Human-centred Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics in emerging higher education: a critical scoping review
Source title: Discover Education
Affiliations: Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait City, Kuwait
Authors with affiliations: Alenezi A.F., Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait City, Kuwait
Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Learning Analytics (LA) are increasingly being adopted by higher education institutions (HEIs) to support student learning, institutional decision-making, and student success. However, most published evidence originates from high-income countries, and comparatively little is known about how these technologies are implemented within the institutional, governance, and socio-cultural contexts of emerging economies. This critical scoping review synthesises the current evidence on AI and LA implementation across emerging higher education systems, with particular attention to educational outcomes, implementation contexts, equity, and institutional readiness. The review followed the methodological framework of Arksey and O’Malley [2] and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Peer-reviewed and selected grey literature published between 2019 and 2025 were systematically searched across major education, computer science, and multidisciplinary databases. Nineteen primary studies met the eligibility criteria, together with one contextual background study retained to inform interpretation of the historical development of AI and LA implementation. The evidence comprised empirical investigations, systematic and scoping reviews, policy reports, bibliometric analyses, and conceptual studies. The reviewed evidence indicates considerable regional variation in both the maturity and emphasis of AI and LA implementation. Studies from Latin America primarily describe collaborative institutional capacity-building initiatives, while evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa focuses on ethical governance, data justice, and responsible implementation. Studies from South Asia predominantly examine predictive modelling with comparatively limited evaluation of pedagogical impact, whereas evidence from East Asia and the Middle East remains exploratory and reflects early stages of institutional implementation. Across the reviewed literature, predictive early-warning systems, adaptive learning platforms, institutional analytics dashboards, and generative AI applications demonstrate potential to support educational decision-making when implemented alongside appropriate human oversight, educator involvement, and governance arrangements. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous, with relatively few longitudinal investigations, limited causal evaluation, and substantial variation in methodological quality. The review identifies algorithmic myopia as a recurring pattern within the current literature, whereby research frequently prioritises predictive performance over educational effectiveness, learner experience, equity, and long-term institutional impact. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes a Human-Centred and Contextually Responsive AI Framework that integrates responsible AI, equity by design, educator participation, and contextual governance to support sustainable implementation in emerging higher education systems. The review concludes with evidence-informed recommendations for higher education institutions, policymakers, technology providers, and international development partners, together with a future research agenda aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Knowledge Graph–AI Agent Collaborative Framework: A Case Study and Effectiveness Analysis of Higher Education Teaching Practice Based on an Integrated Teaching Platform
Source title: Information (Switzerland)
Affiliations: School of Navigation, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, 430063, China; Wenhua College, Wuhan, 430074, China
Authors with affiliations: Liu K., School of Navigation, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, 430063, China; Zhang J., School of Navigation, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, 430063, China; Guan H., School of Navigation, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, 430063, China; Zheng C., Wenhua College, Wuhan, 430074, China; Yang X., School of Navigation, Wuhan University of Technology, Wuhan, 430063, China
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of educational digitalization and generative artificial intelligence, knowledge graphs and AI agents have emerged as key technologies supporting smart higher education. To address challenges in current AI-assisted teaching, including insufficient support from structured knowledge systems, inadequate coordination across teaching processes, and delayed evaluation and feedback, this study proposes a collaborative framework integrating knowledge graphs and AI agents within an integrated teaching platform, and illustrates its integrated operational mechanism for knowledge organization, learning support, learning analytics, and teaching evaluation. Using the core course Nautical Navigation in the Navigation Technology Specialty at WHUT as a case study, the framework was implemented on the Chaoxing Smart Course Platform and applied to 459 students across two cohorts. The implementation achieved knowledge structuring and learning process visualization. The constructed course knowledge graph includes 336 knowledge points and more than 2700 associated learning resources and assessment items, while 30 instructional AI agents were developed and deployed to support different teaching and learning scenarios. The results indicate that the framework improves course knowledge organization, enhances student engagement and self-directed learning, enables visualization of learning processes and precision in teaching evaluation, and promotes a shift from experience-based to data-driven instructional decision-making. Compared with the previous cohort, students’ average daily learning time increased from 564 s to 618 s, participation rates in chapter quizzes, group discussions, and assignment completion all exceeded 90%, and more than 80% of respondents expressed willingness to continue using this learning model. The study provides a practical reference for AI-enabled teaching reform and digital transformation in higher education. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Feedback Dynamics in Agentic LLM-Based Text Accessibility
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Affiliations: TIB – Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology, Hanover, Germany; Università degli Studi di Salerno, Salerno, Italy; KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Digital Futures, Stockholm, Sweden

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to improve the readability and accessibility of educational texts, yet little is known about how such systems respond to iterative feedback over time. This paper studies an agentic LLM within an iterative feedback pipeline and examines how feedback granularity shapes refinement behaviour in readability and dyslexia-oriented text adaptation. We compare holistic feedback, which presents all detected accessibility violations at once, with incremental feedback that targets subsets of criteria across iterations. Using learning analytics measures, we analyse refinement trajectories across four iterations in terms of readability, dyslexia accessibility, and error recurrence. Experiments on 134 history textbook chapters show that both feedback strategies yield significant improvements over the original texts, with most gains occurring after the first iteration. Contrary to expectations from formative assessment theory, incremental feedback does not consistently outperform holistic feedback and produces more variable refinement trajectories. The findings suggest that iterative feedback enables reliable optimization but does not, by itself, produce consistent progressive adaptation across iterations, highlighting the importance of process-level evaluation in educational AI systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Using Large Language Models to Detect Socially Shared Regulation of Collaborative Learning
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, United States; Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, United States; Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; University of Detroit Mercy, Detroit, MI, United States; New York University, New York, NY, United States
Authors with affiliations: Zhang J., University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, United States; Borchers C., Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, United States; Cohn C., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; Srivastava N., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; Snyder C., University of Detroit Mercy, Detroit, MI, United States; Guo S., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; Ashwin T.S., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; Mohammed N., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States; Noh H., New York University, New York, NY, United States; Biswas G., Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States
Abstract: The field of learning analytics has made notable strides in automating the detection of complex learning processes in multimodal data. However, most advancements have focused on individualized problem-solving instead of collaborative, open-ended problem-solving, which may offer both affordances (richer data) and challenges (low cohesion) to behavioral prediction. Here, we extend predictive models to automatically detect socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) behaviors in collaborative computational modeling environments using embedding-based approaches. We leverage large language models (LLMs) as summarization tools to generate task-aware representations of student dialogue aligned with system logs. These summaries, combined with text-only embeddings, context-enriched embeddings, and log-derived features, were used to train predictive models. Results show that text-only embeddings often achieve stronger performance in detecting SSRL behaviors related to enactment or group dynamics (e.g., off-task behavior or requesting assistance). In contrast, contextual and multimodal features provide complementary benefits for constructs such as planning and reflection. Overall, our findings highlight the promise of embedding-based models for extending learning analytics by enabling scalable detection of SSRL behaviors, ultimately supporting real-time feedback and adaptive scaffolding in collaborative learning environments that teachers value. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Strengthening Cultural Intelligence and International Student Engagement With AI
Source title: Strengthening Cultural Intelligence and International Student Engagement With AI
Affiliations: Ikon Institute of Australia, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Ngocha-Chaderopa N.E., Ikon Institute of Australia, Australia
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and student support in higher education, with technologies such as generative AI, adaptive learning systems, learning analytics, and intelligent tutoring now embedded across educational ecosystems. However, much of the AI-in-education literature remains grounded in culturally neutral assumptions, often overlooking the linguistic, cultural, and epistemic diversity of international student populations. As some of the most digitally mediated learners globally, these students navigate AI-enhanced environments in ways that are deeply shaped by context. Addressing this gap is essential to ensuring that AI-driven education systems are inclusive, equitable, and responsive to diverse learning experiences. Strengthening Cultural Intelligence and International Student Engagement With AI positions cultural intelligence as a critical design, pedagogical, and ethical capability for AI-enabled education. This book brings together scholars, learning scientists, educational technologists, and higher education researchers to examine how AI systems can be designed, implemented, and governed in ways that meaningfully enhance international student engagement, equity, and learning outcomes. Covering topics such as the politics of language in global classrooms, intelligent tutoring systems, and academic integrity, this book is a fundamental academic resource for graduate and doctoral students, educational administrators, educational data scientists, EdTech developers, instructional designers, policymakers, and more. Title: Enhancing language learning through adaptive gamification and a multi-agent approach with experience application programming interface and blockchain integration
Source title: PeerJ Computer Science
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, College of Computer and Information Sciences, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; Department of Computer Science, College of Computer and Information Sciences, Jouf University, Jouf, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Hammami S., Department of Computer Science, College of Computer and Information Sciences, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; Alomair Y., Department of Computer Science, College of Computer and Information Sciences, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Department of Computer Science, College of Computer and Information Sciences, Jouf University, Jouf, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: This article proposes an adaptive gamified architecture model for next-generation language learning, driven by the synergistic integration of multi-agent systems, the Experience Application Programming Interface (xAPI), and blockchain technology. The proposed architecture employs intelligent multi-agent coordination to dynamically personalize learning content and e-assessment activities in real time, adapting continuously to individual learners' behaviors and proficiency levels. To enhance engagement and retention, the system integrates card-based gamification mechanics, including interactive challenges and real-time reward mechanisms. The xAPI enables comprehensive learning analytics and interoperability across platforms, while blockchain technology ensures secure data storage and data integrity. A case study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model. The results indicate that participants in the experimental group achieved significantly higher levels of language proficiency and motivation than those in the control group. These findings suggest that the integration of adaptive learning and gamification can effectively enhance language acquisition outcomes, contributing to the advancement of intelligent foreign language learning (FLL) systems. © 2026 Hammami and Alomair. Affiliations: Centre for Research in Digital Education, Edinburgh Futures Institute, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom; Faculty of Arts and Education, University of Stavanger, Stavanger, Norway; Department of Media and Communications, London School of Economics and Political Science, London, United Kingdom; Institute for AI and Robotics, Waseda University, Tokyo, Japan

Abstract: AI systems increasingly shape children's learning, from adaptive platforms and classroom analytics to GenAI used for creative and academic support. Alongside promises of personalisation and engagement, these systems raise persistent concerns for children's rights, including privacy, play, protection from commercial exploitation, and non-discrimination in the presence of bias. This workshop focuses on designing rights-respecting, child-centred AI for learning. Bringing together researchers, designers, educators, policymakers, and practitioners, it examines how concepts such as privacy, participation, play, and fairness can be operationalised in AI design. Through case studies and structured activities, participants will discuss shared design challenges, practical design principles and methods, and identify priorities for future child-centered AI research and practice for the IDC community.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: StoryLensEdu: Personalized Learning Report Generation through Narrative-Driven Multi-Agent Systems
Source title: IEEE Pacific Visualization Symposium
Affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong
Authors with affiliations: Shen L., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Luo Y., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Sheng R., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; He Y., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Li H., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Yang L., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Qu H., The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong
Abstract: Personalized feedback plays an important role in self-regulated learning (SRL), helping students track progress and refine their strategies. However, current common solutions, such as text-based reports or learning analytics dashboards, often suffer from poor interpretability, monotonous presentation, and limited explainability. To overcome these challenges, we present StoryLensEdu, a narrative-driven multi-agent system that automatically generates intuitive, engaging, and interactive learning reports. StoryLensEdu integrates three agents: a Data Analyst that extracts data insights based on a learning objective-centered structure, a Teacher that ensures educational relevance and offers actionable suggestions, and a Storyteller that organizes these insights using the Hero's Journey narrative framework. StoryLensEdu supports post-generation interactive question answering to improve explainability and user engagement. We conducted a formative study in a real high school and iteratively developed StoryLensEdu in collaboration with an E-learning team to inform our design. Evaluation with real users shows that StoryLensEdu enhances engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of the learning process. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Content-Grounded Learning Behavior Analysis for Contextualized Feedback
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan
Authors with affiliations: Shimada A., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan; Miyazaki Y., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan; Hirotaka S., Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan
Abstract: Fine-grained learning behavior analysis based on interaction logs enables detailed investigation of students’ study strategies, but the resulting representations are often difficult for educators to interpret. This study proposes a content-grounded learning behavior analysis framework that generates contextualized feedback by grounding behavior differences in instructional content. Learning behaviors are analyzed independently, while instructional pages are grouped into semantically coherent content clusters that serve as explanatory contexts, and a large language model (LLM) is used solely as an explanation layer to transform fixed analysis results into human-readable feedback. The framework is evaluated using learning logs and lecture materials from real-world university courses through a within-subject user study. Results show that feedback integrating analytical evidence with explanatory descriptions is perceived as more understandable and useful than feedback presenting either component alone. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Automated Essay Marking with Data-Efficient Augmentation and Score-Token Weighted Loss
Source title: 2026 7th International Conference on Computer Vision and Data Mining, ICCVDM 2026
Affiliations: Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Shakaa Y., Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom; Aburumman N., Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom; Anagnostou A., Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom; Taylor S., Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom; Li Y., Brunel University London, Department of Computer Science, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: Automated Essay Scoring (AES) research has predominantly focused on holistic scoring, yet rubric-based trait scoring provides richer diagnostic feedback for both students and instructors. While encoder-based models such as BERT have achieved competitive trait scoring performance, they are limited to score prediction and cannot generate the explanatory feedback that makes rubric-based assessment educationally useful. Large Language Models (LLMs), by contrast, naturally support both scoring and feedback generation within a single unified framework. However, most existing work on fine-tuned LLM-based rubric scoring relies on either large annotated corpora or synthetic data augmentation to achieve competitive performance, limiting practical adoption in settings where neither is readily available. This paper investigates whether a small, carefully balanced dataset of real essays can enable a fine-tuned LLM to achieve competitive rubric-based trait scoring. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using QLoRA on progressively augmented subsets of DREsSNew (371, 478, and 736 essays), targeting under-represented score bands at each stage, and propose a score-token weighted loss function that concentrates the training signal on score-bearing tokens. Data augmentation drives the majority of the performance improvement: expanding from 371 to 736 essays yields gains of +0.042 QWK on Content, +0.021 on Organization, +0.041 on Language, 0.024 on Total. Score-token weighting provides a further modest but consistent improvement, most notably on Content (+0.025). Our best configuration achieves per-trait QWK of 0.631 (Content), 0.612 (Organization), 0.625 (Language), and 0.669 (Total) on the DREsSNew test set using only 736 real essays - remaining competitive with models trained on datasets over 65 times larger while preserving the generative capability needed for downstream feedback generation.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The rapid expansion of digital educational resources has led to fragmented learning environments in which students must manage heterogeneous materials with limited adaptive support. Traditional study planning approaches rely on static schedules and fail to account for individual learning pace and real-time performance, resulting in inefficiency and cognitive overload. This paper presents NeuroSEDA, an adaptive learning workflow engine that integrates large language model-based workflow generation with Transformer-based student monitoring in a unified closed-loop architecture. The system automatically converts unstructured educational content into structured learning workflows and continuously adapts instructional complexity based on observed student interactions. A multi-task Transformer model jointly predicts task difficulty and a continuous struggle score from sequential behavioral data, enabling real-time personalization. To support systematic evaluation, a synthetic student interaction dataset is generated using a Hidden Markov Model that simulates evolving confusion dynamics across diverse learner profiles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Transformer model outperforms recurrent and non-sequential baselines, achieving 89.23% classification accuracy and an R2 score of 0.939 for struggle prediction. These findings validate the effectiveness of attention-based sequential modeling for adaptive learning systems and highlight the potential of closed-loop architectures for personalized education. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: The Algorithmic Turn in K-12 Online and Blended Learning: Is AI a Pedagogical Mirage or a New Foundation for Student Agency?
Source title: Open Praxis
Affiliations: Anadolu University, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Bozkurt A., Anadolu University, Turkey
Abstract: The boundary between online and blended learning in K–12 education is increasingly shaped by algorithmic mediation, raising a central tension: whether artificial intelligence supports student agency or reproduces standardization through new forms of governance. This study reports a computationally assisted critical literature review (CLR) of 31 peer-reviewed articles on artificial intelligence in K–12 online and blended learning. We combine systematic review protocols with text-mining techniques to map dominant intellectual clusters and their conceptual linkages. Specifically, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) is used to visualize proximity-based thematic islands, while lexically connected structures are used to trace relational pathways among core concepts. The analysis identifies five themes organizing the field: predictive governance and the institutionalization of at-risk learners; platformized personalization and agent mediation redefining the blend; automation of assessment and feedback and the efficiency trap; student monitoring and natural language processing as infrastructural surveillance; and acceptance, affect, and trust as emotional conditions of agency. Across themes, the literature emphasizes scalable infrastructures (prediction, platforms, automation, monitoring) more consistently than explicit theorization and measurement of student agency. This paper discusses how these trajectories shift pedagogical authority toward default system logics and provides a synthesized framework of practical translations and governance safeguards to protect learner autonomy in K–12 online and blended settings. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping education by enabling personalized learning and increasing student engagement. The rapid adoption of tools such as ChatGPT, however, raises questions about efficacy, academic integrity, and ethics. This study aims to fill a critical gap by providing a systematic comparative evaluation of classical, deep learning, and transformer-based models for sentiment analysis of ChatGPT-related educational discourse, identifying the best-performing approach, and deploying it in an explainable, user-friendly web application for non-technical stakeholders. This study examines public sentiment regarding ChatGPT in education by using a comparative framework that includes transformer-based model, deep learning, and classical machine learning approaches. Previous research in this area has mainly depended on small-scale surveys or static datasets, often without utilizing modern natural language processing (NLP) techniques. This study aims to fill those gaps by gathering 236,275 tweets related to ChatGPT in education and implementing a systematic benchmarking process. Neutral tweets were removed, resulting in a binary classification of positive and negative labels. The data was divided into an 80/20 split for training and testing. A Naive Bayes model with TF-IDF vectorization served as the classical baseline. For the deep learning tier, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) models with Word2Vec embeddings were used. The transformer tier was represented by a fine-tuned DistilBERT model. The models were evaluated based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The fine-tuned DistilBERT achieved the highest accuracy at 98.81%, indicating a strong performance of transformer-based models compared to classical machine learning and deep learning approaches in this dataset. In contrast, the LSTM model achieved 95.40%, the Bi-LSTM reached 94.66%, and the Naive Bayes model recorded an accuracy of 81.77%. A Streamlit-based web application was developed that integrates LIME-based explainability to make sentiment predictions accessible to educators and policymakers. However, it is important to note that this study is limited to English-language Twitter data and relies on a single-domain, single train-test split; therefore, the results may not fully generalize beyond this context. While these findings are promising, broader generalization warrants further investigation. Future research should explore multilingual datasets, additional social media platforms, and more advanced transformer architectures to enhance generalizability and expand applicability in diverse educational contexts. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Beyond the Veneer of Competence: How Structured Prompting Fosters Knowledge Transfer in LLM-Augmented Education

Authors with affiliations: Lin I.-T., Department of Data Science, Soochow University, Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan; Chiu C.-H., Department of Data Science, Soochow University, Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan; Lin S.-H., Department of Data Science, Soochow University, Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan; Lee K.-I., Department of Japanese Language and Literature, Soochow University, Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan; Huang Y.-S., Department of Data Science, Soochow University, Shilin, Taipei, Taiwan
Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models into technical education exposes a critical fault line between building genuine conceptual mastery and merely outsourcing cognition. We examined this tension by tracking 123 computer science students across three AI-supported assessments and one unassisted final exam, comparing a standard control group against a cohort trained in structured Prompt Engineering (PE). Interaction logs and semantic similarity metrics revealed two drastically different approaches to the tool. Untrained students treated the LLM as a shortcut: 76.6% of their submissions heavily mimicked the model's raw output. While this passive extraction maximized short-term grades, it was strongly associated with a severe cognitive dependency. For this group, higher AI usage correlated with worse performance on the independent final exam. The PE-trained students, meanwhile, paid an early "transition cost."Their initial scores dropped as they took on the higher cognitive load of breaking down tasks and reformulating AI responses. Yet, this early friction paid off. When AI support was removed, the trained cohort retained significantly more knowledge, achieving a much higher Transfer Index (59.0% vs. 48.7%). Our data challenges the assumption that educational interfaces should be seamless. To prevent cognitive offloading, educators must treat prompt engineering not as a technical trick, but as a metacognitive skill that injects the "productive friction"necessary for resilient, independent learning.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: AISSA: Implementation and Deployment of an AI-Based Student Slides Analysis Tool for Academic Presentations

Abstract: Providing timely and actionable feedback on oral presentation slides is challenging in higher education, particularly in large classes where teachers cannot realistically deliver detailed formative feedback before students present. This paper introduces AISSA (AI-based Student Slides Analysis tool), a web-based system that combines large language models (LLMs) and Learning Analytics dashboards to support scalable, rubric-based feedback on presentation slides. AISSA allows students to upload their slide decks prior to an oral presentation and automatically receive quantitative scores and qualitative feedback based on teacher-defined evaluation rubrics. The system analyzes both slide-level features and slide content, generates structured feedback through an LLM (ChatGPT 5.2), and presents the results through interactive dashboards for students and teachers. We tested AISSA on a pilot deployment with 46 undergraduate students in a real academic setting. The results indicate that AISSA is technically reliable, economically feasible, and perceived by students as useful for iterative slide improvement. These findings suggest that combining LLM-based analysis with Learning Analytics dashboards is a promising approach for supporting formative feedback on presentation slides at scale. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: The current teaching method of foreign languages is more and more adopting the method of using intelligent software to observe the learner's behavior and adapt teaching methods accordingly, but the teaching software currently used in the field of English learning still has many limitations such as relying on rigid rule sets or single-pass learning prediction models which cannot track and adapt the learners' learning competence and motivation from one teaching moment to the next. This paper introduces a self-adaptive cognitive AI agent model framework which continuously models the learners' behaviour and then uses a perception-reason-plan-act cognitive loop to select tasks, plan tasks, and make tasks more or less difficult for the learners in reading, writing, listening, and speaking. The framework combines a continuous learner behaviour modelling module with a skill-domain model based on the CEFR framework and a module on self-evaluation which recalibrates the adaptation policy based on observed outcomes. The framework's main behaviour-modelling premise – that the signals of interaction that are continuously captured better predict learner outcomes than profile information – is tested empirically using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), a real, publicly accessible, anonymized collection of 32,593 course enrollments and 173,912 graded submissions. The design premise for the framework is that early, continuously updated behavioural signals can drive timely adaptive intervention, and logistic regression and random forest classifiers based on behavioural features (completion rate, submission timing and score trajectory) exhibit an AUC of 0.958 and 0.965 respectively, predicting at-risk outcomes with materially the same accuracy as behaviour-plus-demographics, and a variant using only the first three submissions reaches AUC 0.853, supporting this premise. The results of these empirical studies are then applied to the proposed architecture for developing English skills, and a roadmap for implementing the architecture and further domain-specific validation before classroom deployment is then described. © 2026, Technical institute of Bijeljina. Title: AI-enhanced gamification in education: an integrative review of trends, impacts, and corrective role potential
Source title: Journal of Computers in Education
Affiliations: Graduate School, Universitas Negeri Yogyakarta, Yogyakarta, Indonesia; Faculty of Education, Technische Universität Dresden, Dresden, Germany

Abstract: While educational gamification successfully drives student engagement, it faces persistent criticism for fostering extrinsic reward dependency, superficial achievement (“fast leveling”), and inequitable learning experiences. This study posits Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a critical corrective mechanism to these structural limitations, repositioning static game mechanics within dynamic, adaptive learning ecosystems. Adopting an Integrative Review methodology based on Whittemore and Knafl’s framework, this study synthesizes 61 empirical and theoretical studies (2003–2025) identified through systematic two-way snowballing. Complementary bibliometric data from Scopus and ScienceDirect reveals an exponential “J-curve” growth in the field, marking a decisive disciplinary shift from computer science architectures to pedagogical applications in Social Sciences. The findings indicate that AI integration mitigates traditional gamification pitfalls by (1) personalizing difficulty through adaptive algorithms, (2) replacing superficial rewards with intelligent, real-time feedback, and (3) enhancing inclusivity for diverse learner profiles. Crucially, this review proposes the “AI Corrective Role Framework,” a conceptual model grounded in convergent evidence that operationalizes how AI acts as a learner-centered function to deepen cognitive retention and as a decision-making instrument for institutional strategy. These insights offer researchers and policymakers a robust roadmap for implementing sustainable, evidence-based, and equitable gamified learning environments in the era of Generative AI. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Pedagogical Agent in an E-Learning Environment
Source title: Computers

Authors with affiliations: Jansone A., Center for Science and Engineering, RTU Liepaja Academy, LV-3401, Liepaja, Latvia; Cīrule Z.A., Center for Science and Engineering, RTU Liepaja Academy, LV-3401, Liepaja, Latvia
Abstract: This study examines the development and pedagogical impact of an AI-based pedagogical agent designed for modern e-learning environments. The research addresses a key challenge in digital education: the lack of personalization and immediate feedback in traditional e-learning systems. AI-driven agents “support and motivate learners through instructional interaction” and provide adaptive, data-driven learning experiences that surpass the limitations of rule-based systems. The study begins with a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020, analyzing 46 publications from 2020 to 2025 to identify current AI architectures, pedagogical roles, and the empirical evidence of learning impact. The findings highlight the growing use of machine learning, deep learning, multimodal analytics, and large language models in educational agents. These systems perform roles such as tutor, coach, evaluator, dialogue partner, and consultant, offering cognitive, metacognitive, emotional, and analytical support. Modern agents “continuously monitor user interaction, analyze engagement, and adapt learning content”, enabling highly personalized learning pathways. The study also presents the design of a multimodal pedagogical agent capable of explanation, task generation, diagnostics, and adaptive feedback. Experimental results with students (n = 20) show improved performance, reduced errors, and higher engagement when learning with the agent. Overall, the research demonstrates that AI-based pedagogical agents enhance learning effectiveness and support autonomous learning in higher education. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Design of a Personalized AI-Powered Flutter UI Learning System Integrating Computer Vision, RAG, and LSTM
Source title: Proceedings - IEEE International Research Conference on Smart Computing and Systems Engineering, SCSE 2026
Affiliations: Informatics Institute of Technology, Department of Computing, Colombo, 06, Sri Lanka
Authors with affiliations: Lakshan K.A.L., Informatics Institute of Technology, Department of Computing, Colombo, 06, Sri Lanka; Silva A., Informatics Institute of Technology, Department of Computing, Colombo, 06, Sri Lanka
Abstract: Mobile application development with Flutter is growing rapidly, yet beginners struggle to translate UI designs into functional code. Existing educational resources and AI tools often focus on isolated widgets or automated code generation, lacking contextual guidance and pedagogical reasoning. To address these gaps, this research proposes a learning platform that integrates multimodal AI for UI understanding, RetrievalAugmented Generation (RAG) for personalized instructional content, and sequential learning analytics (LSTM) for adaptive progress tracking. The system analyzes Figma-based UI designs, mapping visual components to Flutter widgets while providing conceptually grounded explanations. Personalized learning paths are generated using RAG, adapting content depth, pacing, and modality to learner needs. LSTM models monitor interactions, predict knowledge gaps, and recommend targeted interventions. Validation through surveys (N=49) and expert review demonstrates feasibility, alignment with learner needs, and potential improvements in learning efficiency, accuracy, retention, and engagement. Comparative analysis shows the design surpasses existing tools by combining visual analysis, adaptive instruction, progress tracking, and mobile-first accessibility. By unifying visual reasoning, personalized content, and longitudinal analytics, the platform supports scaffolded learning, proactive intervention, and scalable deployment, providing a novel approach to bridging the gap between design and implementation in Flutter education. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in higher education has created a need for high-quality, publicly available benchmarks for automated assessment. Existing datasets often rely on synthetic responses or lack detailed human feedback. This paper presents a multilingual dataset of 3041 authentic student answers to 50 open-ended Computer Science questions, collected from real university assessments during the 2025–2026 academic year. The dataset includes the original student responses (Spanish) and their parallel translations (English), instructor (or teacher) defined ideal answers, blind human grading with qualitative feedback, and structured evaluations from three state-of-the-art LLMs (DeepSeek-chat-V3.2, Qwen-flash-2025-07-28, Gemini-2.5-flash-lite-001) using a unified JSON schema. This resource enables reproducible research in automated grading, feedback generation, and cross-lingual educational NLP. Abstract: Collaboration literacy requires adapting to the evolving demands of group work within complex discussions, making it difficult to develop and assess. Traditional analytics metrics capture behavioral signals while missing the semantic dimensions of how learners approach collaboration and build on each other’s ideas. We present Collaboration Literacy through Artifact Reasoning and Augmentation (CLARA), an agentic analytics system that extracts semantic representations from transcripts as analytics artifacts: concept maps representing emergent ideas and relationships, and collaboration assessment characterizing collaboration quality across seven dimensions. While users explore these artifacts through the dashboard, the same artifacts are indexed into distinct vector database collections for agent retrieval and reasoning. This architecture establishes a human-AI common ground where users and AI can operate over shared representations. Evaluation results show that CLARA produces reliable collaboration quality analysis and, owing to the artifacts serving as knowledge infrastructure, improves both retrieval performance and response quality over transcript-only baselines. Our work suggests that AI-produced artifacts may scaffold human interpretation and ground AI reasoning in learning analytics workflows. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: This study expands on a previous investigation into the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) for essay assessment, moving from the specific context of the Military Institute of Engineering (IME) entrance examination to the large-scale scenario of the Brazilian National High School Exam (ENEM). The methodology compared a state-of-the-art LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) with experts in human classification. The results show that advanced LLMs exhibit excellent reliability (ICC > 0.95) and extremely high overall alignment (r > 0.98) with human assessors. More significantly, the study reveals that the AI’s accuracy is enhanced by structured rubrics like ENEM’s. However, the analysis also identified the persistence of a subtle algorithmic leniency, where the model tends to overestimate the quality of subjective criteria, such as argumentative depth - a limitation already observed in the initial phase of the study. It is concluded that while LLMs are robust automation tools, human supervision remains crucial for calibrating judgments on profound qualitative aspects. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Enhancing Open Learning Environments Through Multimodal AI-Based Learning Analytics
Source title: 2026 5th International Conference on Electronics Technology and Artificial Intelligence, ETAI 2026
Affiliations: Zhejiang Vocational Academy of Art, Zhejiang, 310053, China
Authors with affiliations: Chen N., Zhejiang Vocational Academy of Art, Zhejiang, 310053, China
Abstract: The scalability of Open Learning Environments (OLEs) often compromises personalized support, leading to high dropout rates. While multimodal data (visual, auditory, textual, physiological) offer a holistic view of learning, their effective integration for predictive analytics remains a challenge due to heterogeneity, sparsity, and a lack of pedagogical interpretability. This paper presents a unified multimodal AI framework that addresses these gaps through a cross-modal attention fusion network and a generative resource alignment module. Our model dynamically fuses asynchronous data streams and imputes missing modalities using a teacher-student knowledge distillation scheme. Validated on a dataset of 1,200 learners, the framework achieves a 4.21 MAE in grade prediction (outperforming best baseline by 31%) and an F1-score of 0.892 in engagement detection. Crucially, it provides interpretable insights into Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) phases, demonstrating a 34.7% improvement in SRL behavior identification. The integration of pedagogical constraints ensures that predictions and recommendations-such as dynamically aligned Open Educational Resources (OERs)-are cognitively plausible and actionable. This work establishes a robust, scalable foundation for AI-driven personalization in OLEs, bridging the gap between data-driven insights and effective educational intervention.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Applying multimodal learning analytics to naturalistic recordings of clinical simulations: Towards an accurate and scalable pipeline for automated feedback generation
Source title: Learning and Instruction
Affiliations: Department of Learning Health Sciences, University of Michigan Medical School, United States; School of Information, University of Michigan, United States; Computer Science and Engineering, University of Michigan, United States; Steinhardt School, New York University, United States
Authors with affiliations: Popov V., Department of Learning Health Sciences, University of Michigan Medical School, United States, School of Information, University of Michigan, United States; Nguyen S., Computer Science and Engineering, University of Michigan, United States; Ochoa X., Steinhardt School, New York University, United States
Abstract: Background: Educational audiovisual recordings, spanning domains from teacher training to clinical simulations, often remain underutilized due to the intensive human labor required for comprehensive analysis and timely feedback. Aims: This study addresses this challenge by developing and evaluating a multimodal learning analytics (MmLA) pipeline that integrates state-of-the-art visual, speech, and language models to automatically capture complex communication skills. Sample: 244 medical and social work students practicing breaking bad news in a team-based simulated clinical scenario. Methods: We developed and evaluated the MmLA pipeline, which integrates speech extraction, gaze tracking, and semantic analysis using a Large Language Model (LLM). We empirically evaluated the pipeline by measuring the accuracy of each feature-extraction stage, including diarized transcript generation, visual-attention pattern tracking, and LLM-based semantic evaluation of discourse, against human assessors, and by comparing the final automated predictions with human-generated scores. Results: The developed MmLA pipeline effectively extracts and fuses features from naturalistic videos of standardized patient simulations, approaching human-level accuracy, though diarization remains challenging with a moderate 29.9 % SER (lower is better). The predictive model using behavioral, verbal, and semantic features achieved 81.82 % accuracy in assessing interaction comfort, with eye contact emerging as the most influential predictor. Conclusions: By leveraging the most common multimodal data sources, such as video and audio, the study provides a scalable methodological blueprint that can be adapted to diverse educational settings to foster communication skills. © 2025 The Authors

Title: Tracing Process Alignment in Human-AI-Human Learning: A Learning Analytics Case of GenAI-Assisted Preparation and Peer Feedback
Source title: CEUR Workshop Proceedings
Affiliations: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Unter den Linden 6, Berlin, 10099, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Sun W., Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Unter den Linden 6, Berlin, 10099, Germany
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes embedded in learning activities, learners increasingly engage in multi-phase human–AI–human learning sequences, where AI-supported individual preparation precedes peer collaboration. While prior research has examined learning outcomes and perceptions of GenAI use, less attention has been paid to how ideas developed during human–AI interaction are taken up, transformed, or set aside in subsequent human–human collaboration—particularly from a process-oriented learning analytics perspective. This paper presents a methodological and analytical demonstration for tracing process alignment across such learning sequences, focusing on GenAI-assisted preparation followed by peer feedback dialogue. Using empirical data from student teachers (36 GenAI prompt logs and 18 dyadic peer dialogues), this study illustrates an analytic pipeline that integrates semantic similarity analysis, behavioral coding of feedback roles, sequence clustering, and compact hidden Markov models (HMMs). Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of GenAI or making causal claims, our analyses descriptively characterize how preparatory human–AI interactions relate to subsequent collaborative processes. The results illustrate two distinct interaction profiles: a socially oriented, praise-driven feedback mode and an elaboration-oriented mode characterized by higher semantic alignment between GenAI prompts and dialogue utterances. These profiles highlight different ways in which AI-supported preparation may be appropriated within peer dialogue. We position this work as a contribution to the GenAI–Learning Analytics community by offering reusable analytic tools and conceptual framing for examining process-level dynamics of human–AI collaboration across learning phases. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Title: Read the Room or Lead the Room: Understanding Socio-Cognitive Dynamics in Human-AI Teaming
Source title: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference, LAK 2026
Affiliations: University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Choi J., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Samadi M.A., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Jaquay S., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Park S., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States; Nixon N., University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, United States
Abstract: Research on Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) has traditionally examined how humans rely on one another cognitively and socially to accomplish tasks together. With the rapid advancement of AI and large language models, however, a new question emerge: what happens to team dynamics when one of the “teammates" is not human? In this study, we investigate how the integration of an AI teammate – a fully autonomous GPT-4 agent with social, cognitive, and affective capabilities – shapes the socio-cognitive dynamics of CPS. We analyze discourse data collected from human-AI teaming (HAT) experiments conducted on a novel platform specifically designed for HAT research. Using two natural language processing (NLP) methods, specifically Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) and Group Communication Analysis (GCA), we found that AI teammates often assumed the role of dominant cognitive facilitators, guiding, planning, and driving group decision-making. However, they did so in a socially detached manner, frequently pushing agenda in a verbose and repetitive way. By contrast, humans working with AI used more language reflecting social processes, suggesting that they assumed more socially oriented roles. Our study highlights how learning analytics can provide critical insights into the socio-cognitive dynamics of human-AI collaboration. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Design affordance diagnostic framework: screening construct-irrelevant variance in computational thinking assessment
Source title: Interactive Learning Environments
Affiliations: Department of Educational Leadership, Policy, and Technology Studies, The University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, United States; Department of Teaching, Learning and Culture, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, United States; Department of Education, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea

Abstract: Interactive virtual makerspaces generate process data, but platform affordances can complicate their interpretation as evidence of computational thinking (CT). This exploratory study presents the Design Affordance Diagnostic Framework (DADF), which evaluates indicators through five gates: variance, reliability, association with outcomes, robustness to non-independence and multiple-testing control. Artifacts from two cohorts of pre-service teachers completing a Roblox game design activity were examined. Using LLM-coded CT outcomes, network density showed a positive unadjusted association in 2024 but was not statistically significant when pooled (r =.16, n = 55). Reflection depth showed a positive pooled association (r =.36, n = 55) and remained provisional because of coding reliability limitations. In 2025, logic density showed a positive unadjusted association (r =.40, n = 25) and was retained as provisional; code volume was not statistically significant (r = −.18, n = 25). Available revised-analysis records do not establish cluster-robust or multiplicity-adjusted inference, so full passage through all gates is not established. DADF provides a procedure for identifying indicators that require further validation across cohorts, instruments and platforms. © 2026 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

Title: Mapping the landscape of artificial intelligence and data literacy in education: A topic modelling and text mining approach
Source title: Journal of Research on Technology in Education
Affiliations: Anqing Normal University, Anhui, Anqing, China; Nanjing University, Jiangsu, Nanjing, China
Authors with affiliations: Sun T., Anqing Normal University, Anhui, Anqing, China; Hu R., Anqing Normal University, Anhui, Anqing, China; Yang N., Nanjing University, Jiangsu, Nanjing, China
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes pervasive in education, data literacy has emerged as a foundational competence in AI-mediated learning. Despite increasing research attention, the field remains fragmented, with limited longitudinal evidence on its thematic structure and evolution. Addressing this gap, this study presents a longitudinal analysis of AI and data literacy research from 2005 to 2025 using BERT-based and dynamic topic modeling. Twelve topic clusters were identified, revealing conceptual relationships, temporal trajectories, and citation patterns. Findings show rapid growth in topics related to intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, ethics, and evaluation-oriented data literacy, particularly following the rise of generative AI. Keyword network analysis indicates a shift from data mining and visualization toward AI-driven analytics and educational innovation. © 2026 ISTE+ASCD.

Abstract: This study examines feedback in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing contexts, focusing on written corrective feedback (WCF). Large language models (LLMs) can provide WCF at scale, but aligning them with pedagogical best practices remains an ongoing challenge. WCF meeting criteria like factuality or relevance may still be unsuitable for learning contexts, highlighting the need for extrinsic evaluation based on the learner’s perspective. We deployed WCF systems in a university-level EFL class with nearly 2,000 students, collecting over 20,000 drafts. We evaluated the generated WCF from two perspectives: intrinsic evaluation by experienced English teachers using a rubric, and extrinsic evaluation via student feedback and engagement metrics. Results revealed low alignment between teacher expert ratings and student feedback. These findings suggest that traditional expert evaluation alone may not fully capture WCF’s usability or helpfulness from the learner’s perspective, highlighting the importance of learner-centered evaluation frameworks for AI-based applications in language education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. This conceptual article proposes the SAM model—self-regulation (S), ambiguity tolerance (A), and methodological competence (M)—as a bounded person-level resource model within broader AI readiness, with educators’ AI readiness as a central application. S denotes regulatory capacity, A a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and M the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain M1 and domain-specific M2. SAM’s distinctive claim is configurational: M should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher S and, under high ambiguity, when A is higher. These relations, the M1/M2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. The model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. For AI-based assessment and learning analytics, educators’ interpretations of AI-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. SAM thus offers a research agenda predicting when AI support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Development of UI/UX Dashboard for Student and Class Performance in Basic Accounting Learning on Edu Journal Platform
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Enterprise and Industrial System, ICOEINS 2026
Affiliations: School of Applied Science Telkom University, Telkom University, Bandung, Indonesia

Abstract: Teaching basic accounting in vocational high schools requires teachers to continuously monitor students' conceptual understanding due to the hierarchical and interconnected nature of accounting concepts. However, teachers often face difficulties in efficiently managing and evaluating student learning performance because learning data are scattered, processed manually, and difficult to interpret. This study aims to design a teacher-facing learning analytics dashboard to support monitoring of student and class performance in basic accounting learning on the Edu Jurnal platform. The dashboard was developed using a design-based research approach through the Design Thinking method, consisting of empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test stages. The design process produced several artifacts, including user personas, problem statements, feature requirements, information architecture, and user flow, which were implemented into low-fidelity and high-fidelity prototypes using Figma. The proposed dashboard includes features such as class performance monitoring, student performance grouping, item-level analysis, assignment score summaries, and identification of difficult transaction topics. Conceptually, student performance grouping uses the K-means clustering method, while difficult topic identification utilizes Generative AI to label transaction topics and identify topics with the highest student error rates. The prototype was evaluated through User Acceptance Testing (UAT) involving 14 accounting teachers from two vocational schools in Bandung. The results indicate that the dashboard features and design align with teachers' needs and classroom evaluation practices. This study contributes a user-centered design framework for teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards in basic accounting education and provides a foundation for future system implementation within the Edu Jurnal platform. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly act as proactive collaborators in writing and reasoning tasks. A recurring concern is that such systems may produce strong artifacts while quietly eroding the learner's epistemic agency. This position paper argues that the concern is empirically tractable, and that current evaluation frameworks, which equate output quality with learning success, systematically miss it. Across the cohort, students produced argumentatively defensible policies (mean Argument Defensibility = 70.3) yet exhibited very low Epistemic Ownership (mean = 27.8), with 75.4% of sessions falling into a high-defensibility, low-ownership pattern. Behavioral traces show heavy paste reliance concentrated at the final synthesis stage. We argue that this AD-EO dissociation marks a distinct failure mode of agentic AI in education and propose three design implications for human-AI orchestration: ownership-aware evaluation, friction at ownership-critical moments, and stage-sensitive agency modeling. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly need evidence-based insights to adapt curricula to rapidly changing professional practices. This paper presents an AI-based toolchain that analyzes student internship reports to identify sectoral contexts, work tasks, and competency profiles, enabling data-driven reflection on curriculum-practice alignment. The pipeline combines transformer-based text processing, topic modeling, and embedding-based similarity analysis to extract and compare competencies from 98 internship reports and 99 module descriptions across three interdisciplinary bachelor's programs. Results reveal both alignment between curricular intentions and workplace activities as well as internship-dominant competencies not explicitly captured in curricula. Interpreted through a systems-theoretical lens, internship reports function as a medium of structural coupling between education and the labor market, extending institutional self-observation without replacing academic judgment. The study illustrates how AI-supported analysis can strengthen the reflexivity of higher education and support evidence-informed curriculum development. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: While generative AI lowers the barrier to creating pedagogical agents, unguided designs risk undermining learner agency and exposing learners to hallucinated content. This paper argues that a constructivist framing provides a strong theoretical basis for realigning pedagogical agent design to promote active knowledge construction and problem-solving. Guided by constructivist principles, we propose a design framework that (1) incorporates context-aware, in-the-moment guidance within authentic, open-ended learning activities; (2) supports the development of interpretation through productive cognitive conflict; (3) encourages collaboration and group discussions; (4) allows artifact co-creation with formative evaluation; and (5) fine-tunes cognitive apprenticeship strategies and intervention timing. We demonstrate how agents implement these principles by applying generative AI and multimodal learning analytics across various constructivist learning settings, including science labs, simulations, and computational modeling environments. We also highlight key safeguards essential for designing and deploying responsible pedagogical agents, including roles in collaboration, teacher oversight, prompt-before-answer rules, positive and open attitudes toward agent use, and maintaining activity authenticity. Grounding pedagogical agents in constructivist principles enables effective use of generative AI's capabilities while addressing its risks, thereby supporting deeper constructivist learning. © 2026

Title: The Educational Economics Simulation Hub: Exploring Power Law Signatures in Student Learning, Engagement, and Strategy
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Affiliations: Secondary School “Einaudi-Molari”, RN, Santarcangelo di Romagna, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Silvestri M., Secondary School “Einaudi-Molari”, RN, Santarcangelo di Romagna, Italy
Abstract: This paper presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of the Educational Economics Simulation Hub, a platform of 24 economic simulation games developed and deployed in secondary school classes as both a teaching tool and a research instrument, combining evidence-based learning design with data-driven behavioural analytics. Each simulator immerses students in a concrete economic role, provides immediate feedback, and feeds a nine-competency assessment framework monitored via a teacher dashboard. Analysing 12,349 strategic decisions from 57 students across four eligible simulators, we find preliminary evidence consistent with three Power Law distributions: the Power Law of Practice (β=0.528, R2=0.952), Pareto engagement (α=1.839, R2=0.846), and Zipf strategy frequency (α=2.051, R2=0.829). The platform was built through vibe coding—natural language collaboration with generative AI—showing that teachers without high programming skills can design research-grade experiential learning environments. These findings are exploratory (N=57) and require larger-scale replication. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: AI-Empowered BIM Course Teaching Reform: A Cross-Integration and Project-Driven Approach

Affiliations: Department of Engineering Management, Hunan University of Information Technology, Changsha, China
Authors with affiliations: Liao Y., Department of Engineering Management, Hunan University of Information Technology, Changsha, China
Abstract: Addressing persistent challenges in BIM course instruction-disconnect between curriculum and industry practice, delayed feedback, and insufficient integration of emerging technologies-this study employs the “Building Information Modeling (BIM) Technology Applications” course as a case study to investigate AI embedding strategies across the entire instructional process. The course team developed a “Cross-Integration and Project-Driven” model deploying AI at three stages: pre-class, the SuperStarLearn platform captures preparation data to generate learning analytics; in-class, an AI-powered drawing review tool using Structured Similarity Index (SSIM) image comparison algorithms automatically detects discrepancies between student models and reference standards, reducing evaluation from days to minutes; post-class, students use domestic AI platforms-DeepSeek and Doubao AI-to develop Python scripts (pandas/matplotlib) or Excel formulas (VLOOKUP/SUMPRODUCT) for carbon emission calculation and analysis. Empirical results show final exam scores rising from 71.3 to 76.3 points. The core novelty lies not in any single tool, but in the systematic integration pathway linking pre-class, in-class, and post-class AI applications into a coherent instructional loop-a holistic framework largely absent in prior research. This study offers a replicable framework for integrating AI tools within engineering education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Gamified Learning for EFL Public Speaking: Feasibility, Design Framework, and a Preregisterable Evaluation Protocol
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education, ICBDIE 2026

Abstract: Gamified speaking practice is increasingly common in EFL courses, yet many implementations are difficult to evaluate and may produce short-lived engagement gains. This paper proposes a theory-grounded, AI-assisted gamified framework for university EFL public speaking that combines brief speaking missions with rubric-referenced coaching powered by large language models. Grounded in self-determination theory, the design emphasizes meaningful choice, calibrated challenge, and opt-in social support to support sustained practice while seeking to avoid undermining learner autonomy. We contribute (1) design principles and testable hypotheses linking game mechanics to speaking pedagogy, (2) a modular, prototype-oriented architecture for blended or mobile deployment, and (3) a preregisterable, semester-long evaluation protocol with standardized short academic mini-talk tasks and blinded rubric-based rating with rater calibration. We also outline responsible AI safeguards for audio data, transparency, and teacher oversight. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: With generative artificial intelligence driving the growth of dialogic data in education, automated coding is a promising direction for learning analytics to improve efficiency. This surge highlights the need to understand the nuances of student-AI interactions, especially those rare yet crucial. However, automated coding may struggle to capture these rare codes due to imbalanced data, while human coding remains time-consuming and labour-intensive. The current study examined the potential of large language models (LLMs) to approximate or replace humans in deductive, theory-driven coding, while also exploring how human–AI collaboration might support such coding tasks at scale. We compared the coding performance of small transformer classifiers (e.g., BERT) and LLMs in two datasets, with particular attention to imbalanced head–tail distributions in dialogue codes. Our results showed that LLMs did not outperform BERT-based models and exhibited systematic errors and biases in deductive coding tasks. We designed and evaluated a human–AI collaborative workflow that improved coding efficiency while maintaining coding reliability. Our findings reveal both the limitations of LLMs – especially their difficulties with semantic similarity and theoretical interpretations – and the indispensable role of human judgment, while demonstrating the practical promise of human–AI collaborative workflows for coding. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: GAI-Assisted Digital Content Creation: Effects of Prompting Strategies on Learning Behaviors
Source title: 2026 8th International Conference on Computer Science and Technologies in Education, CSTE 2026
Affiliations: Jing Hengyi School of Education, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhang Q., Jing Hengyi School of Education, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, China; Zou J., Jing Hengyi School of Education, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) technology, its applications are gradually transitioning from tool assistance to creative empowerment. To achieve high-quality GAI content, the academic community has proposed 'educational prompt engineering.' With the assistance of prompt words, GAI's output content will be of greater quality, and the artistic expressiveness of the works will be enhanced. However, few research has looked into how prompt phrases used in GAI digital content creation affect university students' creative behaviors. The researchers chose 122 university students from three classes to undertake a quasi-experimental study on digital content creation in different learning contexts. Lagged sequence analysis, and other methods were used to investigate differences in university students' digital content creation behaviors in traditional technology environments, GAI environments without prompt strategies, and GAI environments with integrated prompt strategies. Research findings: The three groups' creative behaviors differed. The study makes appropriate recommendations on how to better integrate prompting strategies and use GAI to aid in digital content creation, with the aim of providing reference for improving learning effectiveness.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Empowering Formative Assessment: Research Progress and Future Directions
Source title: Proceedings of 2025 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education, ICAIE 2025
Affiliations: Zhejiang Institute of Economics and Trade, Zhejiang, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Yang Y., Zhejiang Institute of Economics and Trade, Zhejiang, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Formative assessment is crucial for achieving a high standard of education, yet it often lacks personalisation and timeliness. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into formative assessment has therefore become a central theme in contemporary digital education research. Based on the Web of Science (WoS) database, this paper employs bibliometric analysis and CiteSpace visualization to examine the literature on generative AI-empowered formative assessment from 2019 to 2025. Annual publication trends, keyword co-occurrences, and thematic clusters are analyzed. The findings reveal a research evolution from”theoretical investigation” to”technological adoption”to”multidisciplinary implementation” with research hotspots focusing on intelligent feedback, large language models, deep learning, and adaptive assessment. Contemporary research, however, still remains constrained by technical dependency, low-quality data, and inherent limitations of foundation models and potential ethical risks. Accordingly, this study proposes a systematic framework comprising four dimensions of object, data, technology, and application to reconstruct learner-centered evaluation paradigms, enable cross-layer coordination, and realize a closed-loop intelligent assessment system. The findings have significant theoretical and practical implications for digital transformation and paradigm reconstruction of educational assessment in the era of AI. © 2025 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Abstract: The advancement of digital technologies and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed learning environments in higher education; while tools such as ChatGPT offer personalized experiences and immediate feedback, their relationship with academic performance remains insufficiently understood in university contexts. This study analyzed the use of technological resources in the AI era, considering frequency of use, perceived usefulness, familiarity, and type of use, as well as their contribution to university students’ academic performance and identifying technological and contextual factors associated with it. A data-mining approach was employed, applying 10 supervised regression algorithms using 10-fold cross-validation, complemented by interpretability analysis using SHAP values to identify relevant predictors. Regularized regression models (Elastic Net; Lasso) showed the best relative predictive performance. The SHAP analysis revealed that the field of study (≈ 0.41) and study cycle (≈ 0.34) are the dominant predictors, while the use of AI for academic writing (≈ 0.10) emerged as the technological variable with the greatest positive contribution to academic GPA within the model. Academic performance was mainly associated with structural factors related to students’ educational trajectories, while AI tools showed a complementary role. The predictive contribution of technology appears to depend more on pedagogical integration than on frequency of use alone. These findings suggest the need to integrate digital strategies into higher education, implementing them in a differentiated manner by discipline and academic level, and promoting the guided and purposeful use of AI and technological resources in learning processes. Title: Using Learning Analytics to Unveil Human–AI Collaborative Patterns Between High and Low Performance Students in Instructional Design Activities
Source title: International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Affiliations: Department of Translation and Interpretation, School of Foreign Languages, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China; Department of Curriculum and Learning Sciences, College of Education, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Fan Y., Department of Translation and Interpretation, School of Foreign Languages, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China; Ouyang F., Department of Curriculum and Learning Sciences, College of Education, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Human-AI collaborative patterns represent the recurring sequences of learning processes that emerge during human-AI interactions in educational contexts. Most research investigated human-AI collaboration as outcome-focused activities. From a learning analytics perspective, this research developed a dual-layered coding framework to identify students’ behaviors and corresponding cognitive content with the purpose of examining the collaborative patterns during instructional design activities. Students were first classified into the high and low-performance groups based on instructional design performances, and then the instructional design competency, behavioral-cognitive patterns and perceptions about GenAI were compared between two groups. Results showed that two groups developed different collaborative patterns despite same AI access. High-performance students demonstrated integrated behavioral-cognitive patterns, using copying as a strategy to transition from content exploration to innovative elaboration. Low-performance students exhibited fragmented behavioral-cognitive patterns. This research challenged assumptions about AI’s equal effects in learning and suggested differentiated scaffolding strategies to support equitable collaboration. © 2026 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.
